name: Earth Lusca
description: Multi-platform backdoors (Linux/Windows). SprySOCKS and KTLVdoor. Targeting government and crypto.

overview: Earth Lusca is a China-nexus cyber-espionage cluster that Trend Micro has been tracking since at least April 2019, when the earliest command-and-control infrastructure now attributed to the group first appeared in the researchers' telemetry. Trend Micro publicly named the cluster in its January 2022 technical brief 'Delving Deep: An Analysis of Earth Lusca's Operations', which stitched together three years of intrusions across Asia, Europe and North America under one operator. MITRE ATT&CK adopted the group as G1006 on 1 July 2022 and cross-references it to TAG-22 (Recorded Future), Charcoal Typhoon (Microsoft) and the CHROMIUM / ControlX legacy Microsoft designations.

The group is unusual among Chinese state-adjacent clusters in that it pursues a dual mandate: traditional political and technology espionage against government, education, media, telecommunications, religious-movement and pro-democracy targets, alongside financially motivated intrusions into online-gambling operators and cryptocurrency trading platforms. Trend Micro's Delving Deep brief lists gambling companies in mainland China, U.S. COVID-19 research organisations and cryptocurrency exchanges as three separate victim buckets in the same infrastructure cluster, and independent MITRE and Kaspersky reporting corroborates the espionage-plus-crypto mix. Victimology also spans religious movements banned in mainland China (Falun Gong and Church of Almighty God-linked NGOs), Tibetan and Uyghur diaspora causes, and Hong Kong pro-democracy and human-rights organisations.

Toolset overlaps heavily with the wider Winnti / APT41 constellation - Cobalt Strike, ShadowPad, Winnti, PlugX and Spyder all appear in Earth Lusca operations - but Trend Micro, MITRE and Kaspersky assess that the operator, infrastructure and preferred tradecraft are separable from those adjacent clusters and warrant tracking as their own group. Earth Lusca-specific families first surfaced by Trend Micro include BIOPASS RAT (a Python backdoor that abuses OBS Studio's live-streaming framework to sniff victim screens, July 2021), FunnySwitch and Doraemon (private backdoors), the Linux-only SprySOCKS backdoor derived from the open-source Trochilus RAT (September 2023) and the multiplatform Golang KTLVdoor backdoor pushed at scale through more than 50 Alibaba-hosted C2 nodes (September 2024). Initial-access playbooks lean on watering-hole compromises of trusted community sites, ProxyShell and Oracle GlassFish exploitation of public-facing servers, and spearphishing with malicious links.

ESET's March 2025 Operation FishMedley writeup collapsed several long-running cluster names - Aquatic Panda, TAG-22, Earth Lusca and Red Dev 10 - into the FishMonger label and independently tied FishMonger operations to the Chinese contractor I-SOON (Anxun Information Technology Co., Ltd.), whose eight employees were indicted by the U.S. Southern District of New York on 5 March 2025. MITRE keeps Earth Lusca (G1006) and Aquatic Panda (G0143) as separate but overlapping groups, and Malpedia collapses them under a shared 'aka' list; the FishMedley disclosure is the strongest public evidence to date that Earth Lusca's operators are on I-SOON's payroll rather than being direct MSS or PLA staff, though vendors continue to caveat the mapping.

attribution.text: China-nexus contractor cluster. MITRE ATT&CK tracks Earth Lusca as G1006 and describes it as a suspected China-based cyber-espionage group; Trend Micro's Delving Deep brief characterises the operators as Chinese-speaking with victimology aligned to PRC strategic interests. ESET's March 2025 Operation FishMedley writeup collapses Earth Lusca with the FishMonger / Aquatic Panda / TAG-22 cluster and attributes the operational team to I-SOON, the Chinese contractor whose eight employees were indicted on 5 March 2025 by the U.S. Southern District of New York for hack-for-hire operations against U.S. religious organisations, journalists, government agencies and foreign ministries between 2016 and 2023.
attribution.note: The Earth Lusca / FishMonger / Aquatic Panda cluster mapping is treated as canonical by Malpedia and ESET, but MITRE ATT&CK still keeps G1006 (Earth Lusca) and G0143 (Aquatic Panda) as separate-though-overlapping groups.

notableOperations.name: SprySOCKS Linux backdoor discovery
notableOperations.summary: Trend Micro's Joseph C Chen disclosed on 18 September 2023 that Earth Lusca had staged a previously-undocumented Linux backdoor on operator infrastructure. Dubbed SprySOCKS, the malware ports the open-source Windows Trochilus RAT to Linux, adds a bespoke SOCKS implementation, and communicates with a Cobalt Strike-derived C2 stager. The samples showed two version numbers, indicating active development.

name: Winnti Group
description: Specialized in supply chain and gaming. Stolen certificates for malware signing. Related to APT41.

overview: Winnti Group is a Chinese state-adjacent cyber-espionage cluster tracked by MITRE ATT&CK as G0044 and also known as Blackfly (Symantec) and, in some vendor taxonomies, Wicked Panda. It is one of the clusters inside the broader `Winnti Umbrella` first framed by 401TRG in 2018 as a family of overlapping Chinese contractor teams that share tooling, code-signing certificates and infrastructure. Kaspersky first documented the group in its April 2013 report `Winnti: More than just a game`, which reverse-engineered a decade-old campaign against online-gaming vendors.

The name `Winnti` is overloaded and deserves careful use. `Winnti` in this ficha refers to the actor (G0044). `Winnti for Windows` (MITRE S0141) and its Linux port are the malware family the actor is best known for: a modular, kernel-mode-capable backdoor first seen in 2010-2011, later shared with adjacent clusters such as APT41 (G0096, MITRE tracks these as separate but overlapping groups) and BARIUM. Additional signature families include ShadowPad (S0596), PlugX (S0013), PipeMon (S0501) and Skip-2.0. Because the malware travelled between clusters, `Winnti activity` in vendor reporting does not always map to G0044 specifically.

The 2020 US Department of Justice indictments of Zhang Haoran, Tan Dailin, Jiang Lizhi, Qian Chuan, Fu Qiang, Sun Kailiang associates and two Malaysian resellers tied the cluster to MSS-adjacent contractors operating out of Chengdu 404 Network Technology Co. (also transliterated Chengdu Si Ling Si / æé½åé¶å). The indictments primarily label the defendants as APT41, but the same operators, tooling and Chengdu 404 infrastructure recur in Winnti Group / Blackfly cases, and Kaspersky, ESET and Symantec treat the two clusters as overlapping.

Operationally, Winnti Group is defined by supply-chain compromises of trusted software vendors: NetSarang Xshell (2017), Piriform CCleaner (2017), ASUS Live Update / ShadowHammer (2019) and a long tail of Asian video-game publishers targeted with the Winnti implant. Espionage sits alongside intellectual-property and code-signing-certificate theft, and later shifts toward pharmaceuticals, semiconductors and Hong Kong universities (ESET, 2019-2020) and materials-science labs (Symantec Blackfly, 2022-2023).

attribution.text: Chinese state-sponsored / MSS-adjacent. The US Department of Justice unsealed indictments in August and September 2020 against five PRC nationals working through Chengdu 404 Network Technology Co., a Chengdu-based front company; two Malaysian resellers (Wong Ong Hua and Ling Yang Ching) were charged separately for laundering the operators' financially motivated intrusions. MITRE, Malpedia, Kaspersky GReAT, ESET, Symantec and 401TRG all associate the cluster with Chinese state interests.

name: Equation Group
description: The most sophisticated known APT. Linked to Stuxnet. Tools leaked by Shadow Brokers in 2017.

overview: Equation Group is the name Kaspersky Lab's Global Research & Analysis Team (GReAT) gave, in February 2015, to a cyber-espionage cluster it described as the most sophisticated it had ever tracked. GReAT presented the group at its Security Analyst Summit in Cancun on 16 February 2015 and published the accompanying Q&A dossier the same day, arguing that the operators had been active since at least 2001 and possibly 1996, ran a modular platform (EquationDrug, later GrayFish) that stored plugins inside an encrypted virtual file system in the registry, and, uniquely at the time, could reflash the firmware of hard drives from at least twelve vendors including Seagate, Western Digital, Samsung, Toshiba, IBM, Micron and Hitachi.

The February 2015 report stopped short of naming a country, but the technical bridges to the US government were immediate. Kaspersky documented that the Fanny USB worm, which used two of the same zero-days later burned in Stuxnet (LNK and Task Scheduler) and predated Stuxnet by roughly two years, shared code and command-and-control patterns with Equation implants — the earliest publicly documented tie between the cluster and the Stuxnet/Duqu lineage the same team had already attributed to Israeli-US operations. Reuters, Wired and Ars Technica reported the group's suspected identity as the US National Security Agency the day the paper landed. The December 2013 Der Spiegel disclosures of the ANT catalog and the internal profile of the NSA's Tailored Access Operations (TAO) division had already described analogous implants — IRATEMONK for hard-drive firmware persistence, FANNY-style airgap tooling — as products of TAO's ANT unit.

Public certainty over the attribution consolidated in August 2016, when the persona The Shadow Brokers released a first cache of Equation Group tooling — Firewall implants such as BANANAGLEE and JETPLOW aimed at Cisco, Juniper and Fortinet devices, plus the FUZZBUNCH exploitation framework — followed on 14 April 2017 by the 'Lost in Translation' dump, which contained ETERNALBLUE (weaponising CVE-2017-0144 in SMBv1), ETERNALROMANCE, ETERNALSYNERGY, ETERNALCHAMPION, EXPLODINGCAN and the DOUBLEPULSAR kernel implant, plus the DANDERSPRITZ post-exploitation environment. Microsoft had already silently patched the SMB flaws in MS17-010 one month earlier on 14 March 2017, prompting Ars Technica and others to conclude the vendor had been tipped off by the US government. Within seven weeks the leaked exploits powered WannaCry (12 May 2017, ~230,000 hosts in 150 countries) and NotPetya (27 June 2017), the two most damaging cyber events of the decade.

Equation Group has no stated mandate; researchers describe it as a signals-intelligence collection platform whose targeting — governments, military, telecommunications carriers, energy, aerospace, nuclear research, financial institutions, cryptographers and Islamic scholars across at least 42 countries with Iran, Russia, Pakistan, Afghanistan, India, Syria and China accounting for the bulk of Kaspersky's victim telemetry — is consistent with the NSA's foreign-intelligence mission. No US government agency has ever confirmed or denied ownership of the tools; the closest official acknowledgement remains the November 2015 White House NEOB Cybersecurity Coordinator statement on the Vulnerabilities Equities Process, and the leaked TAO/ANT documents published by Der Spiegel and The Intercept from the Snowden archive.

attribution.text: Public research consensus places Equation Group inside the US National Security Agency, and specifically inside Tailored Access Operations (TAO). Kaspersky's February 2015 report avoided naming a country but documented code overlap with Fanny, Stuxnet and the ANT-catalogued IRATEMONK implant. Reuters cited former NSA employees on the day of publication confirming the tools were NSA-built. The Shadow Brokers dumps of 2016-2017 released internal TAO framework code (FUZZBUNCH, DANDERSPRITZ) whose filenames and internal strings — including operator handles and build environments — matched the ANT/TAO documents leaked by Edward Snowden and published by Der Spiegel in December 2013. The Intercept corroborated the Shadow Brokers material against a still-classified NSA manual for the SECONDDATE implant in August 2016.
attribution.note: No US government agency has ever formally confirmed or denied ownership of the toolset; the 'NSA TAO' framing rests on independent research (Kaspersky, Symantec), on the Snowden documents (Der Spiegel, The Intercept) and on the Shadow Brokers leaks themselves.

origin.text: Kaspersky dated the earliest Equation Group binaries to 2001, with fragments (the EquationLaser installer) as old as 1996-2001; the group's Fanny USB worm surfaced in July 2008 and was disseminated through mid-2011. MITRE's G0020 entry cites the same 2001 lower bound. Public visibility began with Kaspersky's Cancun disclosure on 16 February 2015; the cluster's tooling continued to appear in Shadow Brokers releases through April 2017.

notableOperations.name: Hard-drive firmware persistence (NLS_933W.dll / EquationDrug / GrayFish)

GrayFish (documented alongside EquationDrug in March 2015) added a bootkit that loaded the platform from the very first sector and stored its virtual file system in the registry. Kaspersky called the capability 'without any doubt the most impressive persistence mechanism' it had ever seen.

techniques.name: Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit
techniques.usage: GrayFish installed a bootkit that took control from the very first sector, decrypted and loaded the platform before Windows started, and kept its plugins in an encrypted virtual file system inside the registry.

techniques.name: Rootkit
techniques.usage: EquationDrug and GrayFish hooked kernel structures to hide files, registry keys, network connections and processes; the DOUBLEPULSAR kernel implant released by Shadow Brokers used SMB backdoor hooks to hide operator sessions.

techniques.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
techniques.usage: All Equation Group platforms encrypt their payloads and configuration with RC5/RC6 or custom substitution schemes; GrayFish stored its virtual file system inside the registry as an encrypted blob.

techniques.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
techniques.usage: Loaders decrypt staged payloads at runtime using RC5/RC6 keys derived from hardware identifiers (disk serial, machine GUID) so samples pulled from unrelated hosts cannot be decrypted offline.

techniques.name: Process Injection
techniques.usage: EquationDrug plugins run inside legitimate host processes via reflective load and thread injection so the on-disk footprint of the malicious code stays inside the encrypted registry VFS.

techniques.name: Software Discovery: Security Software Discovery
techniques.usage: The GrayFish bootkit fingerprints host AV/EDR products at load and either delays activation or swaps in per-vendor plugin variants specifically designed to evade the detected product.

name: APT35
description: Massive credential harvesting via phishing. 2025 data leak exposed internal operations.

overview: APT35 is an Iranian state-sponsored cyber-espionage cluster publicly attributed to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and specifically to the IRGC Intelligence Organization (IRGC-IO) in the November 2021 US Department of Justice indictment of two Iranian nationals tied to the Emennet Pasargad / Eeleyanet Gostar front-company ecosystem. MITRE ATT&CK catalogues the group as APT35 (G0059) with the aliases Charming Kitten (ClearSky, Certfa), Newscaster Team (iSIGHT Partners), Phosphorus and later Mint Sandstorm (Microsoft), TA453 (Proofpoint), Cobalt Illusion (Secureworks), Magic Hound (Palo Alto Unit 42) and Yellow Garuda (PwC).

Public reporting places first observed APT35 activity around 2013-2014, with iSIGHT Partners' Newscaster disclosure in May 2014 exposing a multi-year social-engineering operation that used a network of fake journalist, defence and think-tank personas on LinkedIn, Facebook and Twitter to build trust with US, UK, Israeli and Saudi military and government targets. Consolidation of the cluster under the APT35 identifier followed FireEye/Mandiant reporting from 2017 onward; multiple governments and vendors have since converged on the IRGC attribution.

APT35's mandate is strategic intelligence collection in support of Iranian regime priorities: journalists, dissidents and academics covering Iran; regional adversaries (Israel, Saudi Arabia, the UAE); US and European think tanks, human-rights groups and government officials; and US presidential-campaign staff in both 2020 and 2024. Where the MOIS-aligned MuddyWater or the IRGC-affiliated APT33 lean toward critical-infrastructure and destructive operations, APT35 is overwhelmingly a credential-phishing and mailbox-collection actor with a well-documented sideline in hack-and-leak information operations (the 2020 'Enemies of the People' voter-intimidation site) and occasional opportunistic Exchange/ProxyShell exploitation for follow-on access.

From 2021 onward the group's tradecraft has hardened around bespoke PowerShell backdoors (POWERSTAR / CharmPower), custom Gmail and Yahoo mailbox extractors (HYPERSCRAPE, disclosed by Google TAG in August 2022), the BellaCiao dropper family, macOS variants (NokNok), and multi-persona spear-phishing (TA453) against academic and policy targets. In August 2024 Google TAG and Microsoft each disclosed active Iranian phishing against staff on both the Trump and Harris US presidential campaigns; CISA/FBI/ODNI issued a joint statement (AA24-241a) attributing the activity to Iran.

attribution.text: Attributed to Iran's IRGC, specifically the IRGC Intelligence Organization (IRGC-IO). US Department of Justice indictments in 2021 (2020 election disinformation) and US Department of the Treasury OFAC designations in November 2021 and September 2022 name Emennet Pasargad and its personnel as IRGC contractors. Reinforced by Microsoft (Mint Sandstorm / Phosphorus), Google TAG, Mandiant, ClearSky, Certfa, Check Point Research, Proofpoint and MITRE ATT&CK.

name: MuddyWater
description: 2025 campaign: 100+ government entities. Targeting Middle East, Africa, Europe. Phoenix backdoor.

overview: MuddyWater is an Iranian state-sponsored cyber-espionage group formally attributed by US Cyber Command in January 2022 to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), where it operates as 'a subordinate element' inside the ministry's cyber apparatus. MITRE ATT&CK catalogues the cluster as MuddyWater (G0069), with the aliases Static Kitten (Anomali), Seedworm (Symantec), TEMP.Zagros (Mandiant/FireEye), Cobalt Ulster (SecureWorks), Mango Sandstorm (previously MERCURY, Microsoft), Earth Vetala (Trend Micro), Boggy Serpens (Palo Alto Unit 42) and TA450 (Proofpoint).

The group has been publicly tracked since 2017, when Cisco Talos published the 'Muddying the Water' report describing a Middle East-focused campaign that used weaponised Office documents to deliver a PowerShell backdoor family the researchers named POWERSTATS. Kaspersky, ClearSky, Symantec and Group-IB independently corroborated the actor and its POWERSTATS/Powermud/POWGOOP loader ecosystem between 2018 and 2019. In January 2022 US Cyber Command's Cyber National Mission Force published a set of MOIS-linked malware samples on VirusTotal and named the group publicly, moving MuddyWater from vendor consensus to a government attribution.

MuddyWater's mandate is broad regional espionage for MOIS: government ministries, telecoms, oil-and-gas, defence contractors and NGO/dissident targets across the Middle East, North Africa, Central and South Asia, Turkey, Israel and, from 2022 onward, an increasing focus on European and North American organisations. Unlike its IRGC-linked peers (APT35/Charming Kitten, APT34/OilRig), MuddyWater has shown a persistent tendency to reuse open-source and commercial off-the-shelf tooling â a trait CISA's AA22-055A joint advisory explicitly called out and USCYBERCOM's 2022 disclosure underscored by exposing the group's use of PowGoop, Mori and Canopy alongside publicly available offensive frameworks.

The group's most distinctive contemporary tradecraft is the mass abuse of legitimate remote-management-and-monitoring (RMM) software â Atera, ScreenConnect (ConnectWise), SimpleHelp, Syncro, RemoteUtilities and AnyDesk â as its primary post-compromise C2 and lateral-movement channel. This approach, documented in detail by Group-IB, Trend Micro and Proofpoint from 2020 onward, lets MuddyWater blend into IT-support traffic and bypass EDR heuristics tuned for custom malware. In 2022-2023 Microsoft observed MuddyWater collaborating with a paired actor tracked as DEV-1084 on a hybrid on-premises/Azure AD Connect destructive intrusion, and exploiting Log4Shell in unpatched SysAid instances against Israeli organisations.

attribution.text: Attributed to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) by US Cyber Command in January 2022, which described MuddyWater as 'a subordinate element within the Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security'. Attribution has been reinforced by a February 2022 CISA/FBI/USCYBERCOM/NSA/NCSC-UK joint advisory (AA22-055A) and by Microsoft, Mandiant, Cisco Talos, Kaspersky, ClearSky, Symantec, Group-IB and MITRE ATT&CK.

origin.text: First public documentation of the actor cluster came from Cisco Talos in November 2017 ('Muddying the Water: Targeted Attacks in the Middle East'), which named the group MuddyWater after finding attacker-created folders and command-line strings referencing the term. Palo Alto Unit 42, Kaspersky, ClearSky and Symantec (as Seedworm) independently consolidated overlapping telemetry between late 2017 and 2018. Earlier activity attributed to the same cluster has been documented back to at least 2017; some vendor reporting anchors first observed operations to 2016 based on retrospective sample analysis.

Recurring themes include telecommunications operator compromise as a pivot into subscriber data, targeting of ministries of foreign affairs, and destructive follow-on activity (via DEV-1084) against Israeli victims.

MERCURY obtained initial access; DEV-1084 then abused compromised Azure AD Connect credentials to pivot into the tenant, mass-delete Azure resources and impersonate the victim's admin. This was the first publicly documented case of MuddyWater cooperating with a destructive-oriented affiliate.

name: GALLIUM
description: Specialized in global telecom operators. PingPull RAT, SoftEther VPN abuse. Belt & Road Initiative.

overview: GALLIUM is a People's Republic of China state-sponsored cyber-espionage cluster that has been public since 2018 through the Cybereason Operation Soft Cell disclosure of long-dwell intrusions across more than ten global telecommunications operators. MITRE ATT&CK catalogues the group as GALLIUM (G0093); Microsoft names the same cluster Gallium and later Granite Typhoon under its 2023 taxonomy; Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 tracks it as Alloy Taurus; Secureworks (now Sophos) tracked overlap under Bronze Atlas; Cybereason's original victims file used the codename Soft Cell.

The group's mandate is signals-adjacent strategic intelligence collection: bulk theft of Call Detail Records (CDRs) and metadata from telecommunications carriers, along with targeted espionage against government, defence, financial and mining organisations in countries relevant to China's Belt and Road Initiative â Southeast Asia (Afghanistan, Cambodia, Malaysia, Pakistan, the Philippines, Vietnam), the Middle East (Israel, Saudi Arabia, Turkey), Africa and, from 2022 onward, Russia. Cybereason and TCLAB assess that at least one carrier suffered a multi-year compromise that gave operators access to network engineering, billing and Home Location Register systems.

GALLIUM's tradecraft is heavy on living-off-the-land and commodity Chinese-nexus tooling rather than bespoke implants: China Chopper JSP web shells on exposed WildFly / JBoss / Microsoft IIS servers, Mimikatz and a modified Nbtscan for credential access and internal reconnaissance, HTRAN and SoftEther VPN for pivoting, and a locally-modified Gh0st RAT (BlackMould) plus a Poison Ivy branch (Poison Carp / Windshield). From 2022 the group introduced PingPull, a novel Visual C++ RAT documented by Palo Alto Unit 42 that supports ICMP, TCP and HTTPS transports for command-and-control; Unit 42 later described a Linux ELF variant and a Sword2033 backdoor family in the 2023 Alloy Taurus reporting.

Public reporting has repeatedly linked GALLIUM to campaigns disclosed under other names: Cybereason's 2019 Soft Cell and 2020 DeadRinger follow-ups; SentinelLabs' March 2023 Operation Tainted Love against Middle-Eastern telecommunications, which SentinelLabs assessed with high confidence overlapped with Soft Cell tooling and infrastructure; and continued Alloy Taurus intrusions against Southeast Asian government and Middle-Eastern financial targets documented by Unit 42 through 2023-2024. Mandiant's M-Trends 2024 flagged Chinese telco-focused clusters as a persistent Tier 1 threat, with GALLIUM cited among the actors driving the trend.

attribution.text: Attributed to a People's Republic of China state-sponsored operation. Microsoft's MSTIC 2019 disclosure named GALLIUM as a China-based nation-state actor; Cybereason assessed Operation Soft Cell as 'aligned with the interests of the Chinese government' with 'very high confidence' of APT10 / MSS-linked tooling overlap; Palo Alto Unit 42 tracks the cluster as Alloy Taurus and maintains the China-nexus attribution; Microsoft rebranded the group Granite Typhoon under its 2023 typhoon taxonomy for China-based actors. No public indictment or sanctions have named individual operators to date.

techniques.usage: PingPull HTTPS transport and BlackMould/China Chopper C2 over HTTP(S); Unit 42 also documented HTTPS as the most commonly-observed PingPull mode in production.

techniques.name: Non-Application Layer Protocol
techniques.usage: Distinctive PingPull capability: ICMP-tunnelled C2 that hides command traffic inside ping echo-request/reply payloads, useful on carrier networks that permit ICMP but restrict HTTP egress.

techniques.name: Proxy: External Proxy
techniques.usage: HTRAN and SoftEther VPN clients are used as intermediary hop points to disguise operator IPs; SoftEther is deployed on compromised jump hosts inside victim networks.

techniques.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
techniques.usage: PingPull, BlackMould, Mimikatz variants and Nbtscan are staged onto victims after initial web-shell foothold, typically via HTTP downloads from staging servers registered days before use.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
techniques.usage: CDR archives and credential dumps exfiltrated via the same web-shell / PingPull HTTPS or ICMP channels used for command and control; large batches split across sessions to reduce carrier NetFlow anomalies.

name: APT15
description: Targeting embassies and foreign ministries globally. Graphican malware uses Microsoft Graph API for C2.

overview: APT15 is a Chinese state-sponsored cyber-espionage cluster that has been in continuous public reporting since 2010 and is one of the most heavily aliased actors in the industry. MITRE ATT&CK catalogues it as G0004 with the aliases Ke3chang, Mirage, Vixen Panda, GREF, Playful Dragon, RoyalAPT, NICKEL and Nylon Typhoon. FireEye/Mandiant's 2013 'Operation Ke3chang' paper introduced the Ke3chang name in the context of an intrusion campaign against European Ministries of Foreign Affairs staged around the September 2013 G20 summit; NCC Group re-named the same cluster APT15 in its 2018 RoyalCLI/RoyalDNS report; Microsoft's Threat Intelligence Center tracked it as NICKEL until the group was re-catalogued under Microsoft's weather-themed scheme as Nylon Typhoon in April 2023.

Public reporting has consistently placed APT15 in the Chinese state ecosystem, with a diplomatic and foreign-affairs targeting mandate. FireEye, NCC Group, ESET, Intezer and Microsoft agree that the group targets ministries of foreign affairs, embassies, NGOs and defence contractors in Europe, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America, and has been observed since at least 2010. In December 2021 Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit obtained a court order in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia to seize 42 domains that NICKEL was using as command-and-control infrastructure, effectively dismantling that generation of the group's operational network.

The group's tooling has evolved through several distinct generations: BS2005 and MyWeb in the early Ke3chang campaigns (2010-2013); Mirage and MirageFox in 2014-2018; RoyalCLI and RoyalDNS against a UK government service contractor in 2016-2017; Ketrican (from 2015) and its 2017 offshoot Okrum documented by ESET against Slovak, Czech, Belgian, Chilean, Guatemalan and Brazilian diplomatic targets; Neoichor and its Leeson/NumbBoat variants under the NICKEL cryptonym; and, from late 2022, the Graphican backdoor, which uses the Microsoft Graph API and OneDrive as a command-and-control dead-drop, publicly documented by Symantec's Threat Hunter Team in June 2023. Where China-nexus peers such as APT10 or APT41 mix espionage with intellectual-property theft and, in APT41's case, financially motivated intrusions, APT15's reporting is consistently pure espionage.

attribution.text: Attributed to the People's Republic of China. MITRE ATT&CK's Ke3chang group page describes it as 'a threat group attributed to actors operating out of China', and identifies it with APT15, Mirage, Vixen Panda, GREF, Playful Dragon, RoyalAPT, NICKEL and Nylon Typhoon. Microsoft's December 2021 court filing to seize 42 NICKEL domains, and the corresponding MSTIC 'NICKEL targeting government organizations across Latin America and Europe' report, name China as the country of origin and align the cluster with the actor Mandiant, NCC Group and ESET had tracked as Ke3chang / APT15. No individual operatives have been publicly indicted at the time of writing.

MITRE ATT&CK catalogues MirageFox as S0280 and links its use to G0004. The write-up came weeks after NCC Group had described the same operator as 'alive and strong'.

sources.title: MirageFox: APT15 Resurfaces With New Tools Based On Old Ones

notableOperations.name: Okrum & Ketrican against European MFAs
notableOperations.summary: ESET's 2019 white paper documented a Ke3chang backdoor family it named Ketrican (from 2015) and a previously undocumented backdoor named Okrum (from December 2016), deployed against the Ministries of Foreign Affairs of Slovakia, Belgium, Chile, Guatemala and Brazil. The Okrum loader hid its executable content in a PNG steganography wrapper and was delivered by Ketrican, tying the two families to the same operator.

sources.title: Okrum and Ketrican: An overview of recent Ke3chang group activity

notableOperations.name: APT15 Xbash-adjacent post-exploitation ('out of hand tools')
notableOperations.summary: Mandiant's 2019 briefing on APT15 documented a shift to abusing off-the-shelf tools (open-source utilities, WMI, PsExec, PowerShell, native LOLBins) alongside its custom BS2005 / RoyalCLI / MirageFox families, and mapped the group's tradecraft against ATT&CK. The paper is one of the last major public reports before the NICKEL cryptonym takes over from 2020.

sources.title: APT15 Uses Out-of-the-Box Tools to Perform Espionage

notableOperations.name: NICKEL: Latin American and European government targeting (Neoichor / Leeson / NumbBoat)
notableOperations.summary: Microsoft's Threat Intelligence Center reported NICKEL's long-running intrusions against government agencies, diplomatic organisations and NGOs across Central and South America, the Caribbean and Europe, using the Neoichor, Leeson and NumbBoat malware families and living-off-the-land tradecraft (Mimikatz, WDigest tampering, comsvcs.dll LSASS dumping). MSTIC also tied initial access to unpatched Exchange and SharePoint servers and to VPN-appliance credential compromise.

sources.title: NICKEL targeting government organizations across Latin America and Europe

notableOperations.name: Microsoft DCU domain seizure (42 domains)
notableOperations.summary: On 2 December 2021 Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit filed suit in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia against 'John Does 1-2 d/b/a NICKEL' and obtained an ex-parte order allowing it to seize 42 domains that NICKEL was using as command-and-control infrastructure. The takedown was announced publicly on 6 December 2021 and remains the only formal legal action against APT15 to date. The Notice of Pleadings docket carries the complaint, order and the redirected domains list.

name: Naikon
description: Espionage in South China Sea nations. Territorial disputes. Nebulae backdoor.

overview: Naikon is a Chinese state-sponsored cyber-espionage group that has run a long, quiet campaign against the governments, militaries and diplomatic services of the ASEAN littoral states for at least fifteen years. Kaspersky introduced the Naikon cryptonym in a pair of 2015 reports; CrowdStrike tracks the same cluster as Lotus Panda (earlier also styled Override Panda), MITRE ATT&CK catalogues it as G0019, and IBM X-Force ITG06. Public reporting first pinned the group's activity to at least 2010.

The most consequential attribution work is the September 2015 'Project CameraShy' report jointly published by ThreatConnect and Defense Group Inc. (DGI), which used a mix of technical pivot analysis on Naikon C2 infrastructure, HUMINT-style OSINT on a handle called 'greensky27' and open-source Chinese-language military documents to place the operator inside the People's Liberation Army Chengdu Military Region Second Technical Reconnaissance Bureau, Military Unit Cover Designator 78020, based in Kunming, Yunnan. That attribution has been carried forward, verbatim, by MITRE ATT&CK's G0019 page.

Naikon's mandate is regional geopolitical intelligence with a heavy South China Sea flavour: ministries of foreign affairs, defence ministries, presidential and prime-ministerial offices, military commands and diplomatic missions of Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos, Singapore and Nepal, plus embassies of border states hosted in the region. Where APT30 (a distinct but adjacent PRC cluster documented by FireEye) shared some of the same regional targets, Naikon is a separate, longer-lived operation with its own tooling.

Tradecraft has evolved but the core recipe has not. Early MsnMM-era campaigns (2010-2015) relied on Office-exploit spearphishing (CVE-2012-0158) dropping SslMM, WinMM, Sys10, Naikon.Downloader / Wnisen and the RARSTONE / RarStone RAT documented by Trend Micro in 2013. From 2019 onward Check Point and Bitdefender documented a fresh generation of loaders and backdoors Ã¢ Aria-body (aria-body-loader), Nebulae, RainyDay, FoundCore Ã¢ delivered through DLL side-loading against legitimate signed binaries, with C2 sometimes tunnelled through compromised diplomatic missions of one victim country used as jump hosts to reach the next. In April 2022 Cluster25 published 'The Lotus Panda is Awake, Again', documenting continued Naikon activity against Southeast Asian government targets with an updated RainyDay/FoundCore variant.

attribution.text: Attributed to the People's Liberation Army Chengdu Military Region Second Technical Reconnaissance Bureau, Military Unit Cover Designator 78020 (Kunming, Yunnan). The core attribution work is the September 2015 joint ThreatConnect / Defense Group Inc. 'Project CameraShy' report, which combined C2 pivot analysis, OSINT on the 'greensky27' persona and open-source Chinese-language military documents. MITRE ATT&CK G0019 lists Unit 78020 as the Naikon operator, and Kaspersky, Check Point and Bitdefender track the same cluster.

Trend Micro's 2013 report on the RARSTONE RAT and Kaspersky's 2015 Hellsing report describe the same operator under the earliest publicly documented campaigns.

notableOperations.name: RARSTONE / Naikon Southeast Asian phishing
notableOperations.summary: Trend Micro publicly documented the RARSTONE RAT in February 2013 after observing waves of Office-exploit spearphishing against diplomatic and industry targets across Vietnam, India, Malaysia, Nepal, Singapore and the Philippines. The RARSTONE / RarStone family is one of the earliest publicly named pieces of Naikon tooling and remained a fixture of the toolkit through 2014.

notableOperations.name: MH370 tragedy spearphishing
notableOperations.summary: Within days of the March 2014 disappearance of Malaysia Airlines flight MH370, Naikon began spearphishing regional governments and airlines with MH370-themed decoys carrying WinMM / SslMM payloads. The campaign is one of the more widely cited illustrations of the group's opportunistic use of major regional news events.

notableOperations.name: Hellsing counter-intelligence retaliation

The episode is one of the few publicly documented APT-on-APT engagements and remains a canonical illustration of Naikon's counter-intelligence posture.

name: Gamaredon
description: Most active group against Ukraine. GamaWiper. Collaboration with Turla 2025. Cloudflare C2 tunneling.

overview: Gamaredon is a Russian state-sponsored cyber-espionage group focused almost exclusively on Ukraine. In November 2021 the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) publicly attributed the group to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) â specifically the '18th Center for Information Security' (Center 18), operating out of the FSB's Crimean Directorate in occupied Simferopol â and named five FSB officers as members. Ukrainian prosecutors said the officers had conducted more than 5,000 cyberattacks against Ukrainian state bodies since 2014. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the cluster as G0047 (Gamaredon Group / Primitive Bear / ACTINIUM / Armageddon / Shuckworm / DEV-0157 / Aqua Blizzard / NastyShrew / IRON TILDEN), with Palo Alto Unit 42 additionally publishing the name Trident Ursa and CrowdStrike tracking the same cluster as Winterflounder.

Public activity dates to at least 2013, initially detected by ESET, LookingGlass and Symantec as a distinctly noisy, high-volume actor. Unlike its more surgical FSB peer Turla or the GRU's APT28 and Sandworm, Gamaredon is optimised for tempo rather than stealth: SBU counted 5,000+ attacks by 2021, ESET routinely observes thousands of malicious samples per week during Ukrainian working hours, and CERT-UA has published dozens of Gamaredon (UAC-0010) technical bulletins since 2022.

The group's mandate is broad-front tactical espionage against Ukrainian government, military, law enforcement, judiciary, and critical infrastructure targets: intelligence collection to support Russian military operations, credential and document theft, and â after Russia's February 2022 invasion â persistent access to targets of interest to Russian forces on the ground. Spearphishing with Ukrainian-language decoys (troop movements, judicial subpoenas, tax filings) delivers a rotating cast of loosely-coupled remote administration tools written mostly in VBScript, PowerShell, C# and .NET: Pterodo / Pteranodon, GammaLoad, GammaSteel, GammaDrop, PteroLNK, PteroPSDoor, PteroGraphin and dozens of variants ESET catalogues under the Ptero* naming convention.

Since 2022 the operational tempo has been extraordinary. ESET's 2022-2023, 2024 and 2025 reviews document a steady shift toward abusing legitimate cloud services â Cloudflare Tunnels and Workers, Microsoft dev tunnels, Telegram, Telegraph, Teletype, Dropbox, GoFile, DEV Community, Mastodon, Wasabi and Tebi â as C2 dead-drop resolvers and exfiltration destinations, largely as an evasion measure against Ukrainian defender blocklists. In early 2025 ESET publicly documented the first observed hand-off between Gamaredon and Turla on a small number of Ukrainian machines, with Gamaredon's PteroGraphin used to (re)launch Turla's Kazuar v3 backdoor â the first evidence of operational cooperation between the two FSB clusters.

attribution.text: Attributed to Russia's FSB Center 18 (Center for Information Security), operating from the FSB's Crimean Directorate in Simferopol. Attribution was made formally by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) on 4 November 2021, which named five FSB officers and released a technical report tying the operators to over 5,000 attacks on Ukrainian state bodies. The attribution is reinforced by MITRE ATT&CK, Microsoft (ACTINIUM / Aqua Blizzard), Palo Alto Unit 42 (Trident Ursa), ESET, Mandiant, Symantec (Shuckworm) and CERT-UA (UAC-0010).

name: Moses Staff
description: Destructive anti-Israel attacks. DCSrv wiper, PyDCrypt, StrifeWater RAT. Exfiltration and public leaks.

overview: Moses Staff is an Iranian state-linked destructive-attack cluster that emerged publicly in September 2021 with a Telegram channel and .onion leak site claiming to 'expose the crimes of Zionists in occupied Palestine'. Check Point Research first documented the group in November 2021, characterising it as a politically motivated operation whose 'hacktivist' branding masked state sponsorship. IBM Security X-Force independently disclosed the same activity in December 2021 under the name of a wiper campaign against Israeli organisations.

The group's defining tradecraft is a Python-wrapped encryption launcher named PyDCrypt that deploys DCSrv, a Windows service built around the open-source DiskCryptor volume-encryption driver. Unlike criminal ransomware, DCSrv is used for sabotage: Check Point's reverse-engineering showed the operators never intended to provide a decryption path, and the ransom note demanded no payment but instead pointed victims to the Moses Staff propaganda channels. In January 2022 Cybereason disclosed a companion component, the StrifeWater remote-access trojan (also tracked as Broken Fluffy), used for reconnaissance and screenshot collection before the destructive stage.

Secureworks (Counter Threat Unit) tracks the same cluster as Cobalt Sapling and, in a January 2023 note republished by Sophos after the 2025 Secureworks acquisition, tied the November-2022 Abraham's Ax persona targeting Saudi ministries to the same operators. Mandiant's June 2022 profile of the group, published on the Mandiant Advantage blog and now hosted at cloud.google.com, treats Moses Staff as a 'likely Iranian threat actor' conducting politically motivated disruptive activity against Israel; Microsoft internally files related activity under the DEV-0500 identifier. This ficha treats Moses Staff, Cobalt Sapling and Abraham's Ax as aliases for the same cluster.

attribution.text: Attributed to Iranian state interests by Check Point Research, IBM Security X-Force, Mandiant, Cybereason and Secureworks / Sophos. No US, EU or Israeli-government charging document has named individual operators; the vendor consensus is that Moses Staff is a state-directed sabotage cluster rather than an authentic hacktivist collective, based on tradecraft, target selection aligned with Iranian regime priorities, and infrastructure overlaps with other Iranian groups.
attribution.note: No formal government indictment; vendor and community consensus only.

name: Agrius
description: Wiper disguised as ransomware. Fantasy wiper, Apostle, MultiLayer. Supply chain against diamonds globally.

overview: Agrius is an Iran-aligned threat actor first surfaced by SentinelLabs in May 2021 and formally catalogued as MITRE ATT&CK group G1030 in 2024. The cluster is tracked under multiple aliases by different vendors: Pink Sandstorm (Microsoft), AMERICIUM (older Microsoft cryptonym), Agonizing Serpens (Palo Alto Unit 42) and BlackShadow (Israeli press and Clearsky). Public reporting links Agrius to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS).

The group's defining trait is destruction disguised as extortion: wipers (Apostle, DEADWOOD, Fantasy, MultiLayer, PartialWasher, BFG Agonizer) are packaged with ransomware notes, and where a real encryptor exists (Apostle's later variants, and the 2023 Moneybird strain) monetisation is secondary to reputational damage. Stolen data is dumped on social media and Telegram under BlackShadow-style personas rather than sold, and encryption is often unrecoverable by design.

Targeting is overwhelmingly Israeli, with occasional spill-over to organisations connected to Israeli supply chains — the 2022 Fantasy campaign hit an Israeli software developer whose customers included diamond-industry firms in South Africa and Hong Kong. From 2020 the BlackShadow persona has repeatedly hit Israeli tourism, insurance and healthcare (Shirbit, Cyberserve/Atraf, Hillel Yaffe Medical Center); the 2023 Agonizing Serpens campaign broadened into Israeli technology and higher-education.

attribution.text: Iran-aligned, assessed with high confidence by SentinelLabs, ESET, Check Point Research and Palo Alto Unit 42; publicly linked to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) by MITRE ATT&CK. The BlackShadow persona overlaps with the same cluster per multiple vendors.

name: Whitefly
description: SingHealth Singapore breach 2018 (1.5M records). Targeting mainly Singapore. Possibly inactive.

overview: Whitefly is a cyber-espionage cluster first documented by Symantec's Threat Hunter Team in March 2019 as the group behind the July 2018 SingHealth breach, Singapore's largest-ever data-security incident. Between mid-2017 and mid-2018 Whitefly ran a wider intrusion set against Singapore-based organisations in healthcare, media, telecommunications and engineering, with the SingHealth patient database as its highest-profile catch.

The SingHealth intrusion exfiltrated the non-medical personal records of roughly 1.5 million patients and the outpatient dispensed-medicine records of about 160,000 individuals, including then Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong, who the Singapore Committee of Inquiry concluded was a specific target of the attackers. The four-member Committee of Inquiry chaired by former chief district judge Richard Magnus published its Public Report on 10 January 2019, characterising the perpetrator as a well-resourced Advanced Persistent Threat but stopping short of naming a country. Symantec's public attribution to the Whitefly cluster followed two months later.

Whitefly's tradecraft, as documented by Symantec, centres on a custom loader (Vcrodat) delivered by a malicious .exe or .dll disguised as a document and staged via DLL search-order hijacking against filenames borrowed from legitimate security-vendor binaries. A second custom loader, Nibatad, appeared in a subset of intrusions and behaved similarly but was not seen co-resident with Vcrodat. Post-exploitation the group leaned on Mimikatz for credential dumping, an open-source exploit for CVE-2016-0051 to escalate on unpatched Windows hosts, and the Termite hacktool to shepherd multiple compromised machines at once. The same toolset was also observed in intrusions in the wider Southeast Asian defence, telecoms and energy sectors, and against a UK hospitality target - although Symantec noted the latter cases may reflect toolkit-sharing rather than direct Whitefly operations.

Public reporting has treated Whitefly as most likely China-nexus, based on target-set alignment with Chinese strategic and political interests around Singapore and toolset overlap with earlier Symantec-tracked Chinese clusters, but neither the Singapore Committee of Inquiry, MITRE nor Symantec have publicly named a sponsoring state. No new intrusions have been publicly attributed to Whitefly since 2019, and MITRE's G0107 entry has not added activity since the original 2020 write-up.

attribution.text: State-sponsored espionage cluster; Symantec and MITRE stop short of naming a country. The Singapore Committee of Inquiry described the actor as a well-resourced APT operating on behalf of a nation-state. Public reporting and third-party profiles have linked the group to Chinese strategic interests based on target selection and toolset overlap with earlier Symantec-tracked China-nexus clusters, but no government has issued a formal country-level attribution for the SingHealth intrusion.
attribution.note: No public government attribution to a specific country; the 'China-nexus' framing rests on target-set analysis and toolset overlap, not on canonical government or MITRE sourcing.

name: Sidewinder
description: Targeting Pakistan, China, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh. Mediterranean ports. India-Pakistan conflict escalation 2025.

overview: Sidewinder is a long-running espionage cluster active since at least 2012 and publicly attributed to Indian interests by every major vendor that has tracked it. MITRE ATT&CK catalogues the group as SideWinder (G0121); public reporting also uses the aliases Rattlesnake / RattleSnake (Group-IB, Tencent), Razor Tiger (CrowdStrike), T-APT-04 (Tencent), APT-C-17 (Qihoo 360), Hardcore Nationalist (HN2), BabyElephant and APT-Q-39.

The group's primary targets are Pakistani military, government, law-enforcement and diplomatic entities, together with Chinese, Nepalese, Sri Lankan, Bangladeshi and Afghan government and defence organisations. Group-IB's 2023 infrastructure hunt named the State Bank of Pakistan, Sindh and Punjab Police, the Federal Investigation Agency, the Pakistan Navy and Pakistan Air Force, the National Tariff Commission and Tsinghua University in China among documented victims. Kaspersky's October 2024 'Beyond the Surface' report documented an expansion into the Middle East and Africa, including ministries of foreign affairs, port infrastructure, oil traders and telecommunications operators across Bangladesh, Djibouti, Jordan, the Maldives, Myanmar, Nepal, Saudi Arabia, Sri Lanka, Turkey and the UAE, plus diplomatic missions in China, India, Indonesia and Morocco.

Sidewinder's mandate is strategic espionage in service of India's regional intelligence priorities: the Line of Control conflict with Pakistan, Chinese Belt-and-Road exposure in South Asia and, more recently, maritime chokepoints in the western Indian Ocean and Mediterranean. Kaspersky has repeatedly named Sidewinder the most prolific spearphishing actor its telemetry sees, with unique-sample counts in the low-thousands per quarter â a very high tempo sustained through a compact toolkit built on old Microsoft Office exploits (CVE-2017-11882 in particular), mshta-driven HTA loaders and, since late 2023, a modular post-exploitation platform Kaspersky calls StealerBot.

Tradecraft is deliberately unflashy. Initial access is almost always spearphishing with a weaponised RTF or LNK attachment, or a link to server-side-polymorphic HTA landing pages hosted on typosquat domains that impersonate the victim's own ministry, military branch or the news portals they read. Post-exploitation stages rely on DLL side-loading against signed binaries, VBScript / JavaScript / PowerShell chains, Registry Run-key persistence and HTTPS beacons to short-lived C2. The group is notable for how quickly it rebuilds tooling â the ETDA / Thai CERT card and Kaspersky trends reports document continuous minor iterations rather than long-lived binaries.

attribution.text: Attributed to India (suspected) by every major vendor that tracks the cluster; there is no US, EU or Indian-government charging document naming Sidewinder operators. Kaspersky's first public profile in April 2018 stated 'low confidence that this malware might be authored by an Indian company', and subsequent Kaspersky, Group-IB, AT&T Alien Labs, Trend Micro and Cisco Talos reporting has consistently kept the Indian-nexus attribution while stopping short of naming a specific Indian intelligence service.
attribution.note: No formal government attribution; vendor consensus only.

name: Patchwork
description: Espionage against Pakistan and China. EyeShell backdoor, VajraSpy RAT. Honey-trap romance scams on Android.

overview: Patchwork, also tracked as Dropping Elephant (Kaspersky), Chinastrats (Kaspersky), APT-C-09 (Qihoo 360), MONSOON (Forcepoint), Quilted Tiger (CrowdStrike), TG-4410 (SecureWorks) and the Hangover Group, is an India-nexus cyber-espionage cluster active in the public record since at least 2015. Cymmetria's July 2016 Unveiling Patchwork report, together with the Kaspersky GReAT Dropping Elephant paper published the same month, first exposed the actor as a persistent collector operating against foreign-policy establishments interested in China, Pakistan and the wider Indian Ocean region.

The group is publicly regarded as India-sponsored or India-aligned. Attribution is inferential rather than legal (no indictment or sanctions have ever named a Patchwork operator or front company): analysts point to India-based development timezones, Hindi comments, ISP-of-origin telemetry seen by Kaspersky, target lists that consistently prioritise Pakistan and China, and heavy reuse of publicly available offensive tooling. The Hangover / Operation Hangover 2013 investigation by Norman is generally treated as the same crew's earlier incarnation.

Patchwork's tradecraft is best summed up by the moniker itself: much of its malware and delivery code is stitched together from copy-pasted forum snippets, leaked frameworks and open-source tooling. Its custom malware family BADNEWS (and later variants Ragnatela, BackConfig, NDiskMonitor, TINYTYPHON, PubPRISM, PGoShell, EyeShell) sits alongside off-the-shelf QuasarRAT, LokiBot, PowerSploit, Brute Ratel C4 and (on Android) VajraSpy. Initial access is almost always spearphishing with weaponised documents exploiting old Office CVEs â CVE-2012-0158, CVE-2015-1641, CVE-2017-0199, CVE-2017-8570 and CVE-2017-11882 recur across a decade of campaigns.

Targeting is stable and geopolitically legible: Pakistani military, atomic energy and diplomatic entities; Chinese think tanks and academics working on South China Sea, Belt and Road and Tibetan issues; South and Southeast Asian governments (Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Cambodia); occasional Middle-Eastern and Turkish defence programmes; and a recurring 2018-2021 pivot against US think tanks (CFR, CSIS, MERICS impersonations). The July 2025 Arctic Wolf disclosure of Patchwork intrusions into Turkish precision-guided-missile manufacturers is the most recent well-documented campaign at the time of writing.

attribution.text: India-nexus, state-aligned cyber-espionage. Attribution is inferential: no US, EU or Indian legal instrument has ever named a Patchwork operator, but Kaspersky, Cymmetria, Forcepoint, Trend Micro, Volexity, ESET and Arctic Wolf independently converge on an India-based actor whose tasking tracks Indian strategic interests against China, Pakistan and Turkey.

name: Salt Typhoon
description: PRC state-sponsored espionage cluster responsible for the Oct-Dec 2024 breaches of at least nine US telecommunications carriers (AT&T, Verizon, Lumen, T-Mobile, Charter, Windstream, Consolidated, Viasat, and others), the lawful-intercept portal compromise, and the earlier GhostEmperor / FamousSparrow / Earth Estries campaigns in Southeast Asia. Assessed by CISA, FBI, NSA and 12 allied agencies as an MSS-linked global espionage program.

overview: Salt Typhoon is a People's Republic of China (PRC) state-sponsored cyber-espionage group active since at least 2019 and formally attributed to the Ministry of State Security (MSS) by a joint FBI/CISA/NSA advisory in August 2025 (AA25-239a). Microsoft's weather-themed naming scheme uses 'Salt Typhoon'; MITRE ATT&CK canonicalised the actor as G1045 in February 2025, consolidating multiple prior clusters â GhostEmperor (Kaspersky, 2021), FamousSparrow (ESET, 2021), Earth Estries (Trend Micro, 2023), and Recorded Future's RedMike â under a single actor page.

The group's public profile changed decisively in October 2024, when the Wall Street Journal and Washington Post reported that Salt Typhoon had spent months inside the networks of major US telecommunications carriers â AT&T, Verizon and Lumen â reaching not only call detail records but the lawful-intercept portals that carriers operate to serve US law enforcement wiretap requests. Subsequent reporting confirmed T-Mobile, Charter/Spectrum, Consolidated Communications, Windstream and others were also compromised; the FBI later confirmed roughly 150 named high-value targets had communications actively intercepted, including personnel from both the Harris and Trump 2024 presidential campaigns.

The tradecraft is heavily focused on network edge devices and living-off-the-land techniques. Cisco Talos's Feb 2025 'Weathering the Storm' analysis documented that Salt Typhoon obtained initial access to Cisco IOS XE routers primarily through stolen credentials and, in a subset of cases, exploitation of CVE-2018-0171 (Smart Install), then pivoted for months across carrier backbones by editing device configurations, capturing sensitive traffic, and abusing GRE / IPsec tunnels between compromised routers to move laterally. Recorded Future's Insikt Group tracked a separate RedMike sub-cluster that opportunistically exploited CVE-2023-20198 and CVE-2023-20273 against 1,000+ unpatched Cisco devices between December 2024 and January 2025.

Historically, the same cluster ran the GhostEmperor Demodex kernel-mode rootkit campaign that Kaspersky exposed in September 2021 against Southeast Asian governments and telecoms, the FamousSparrow SparrowDoor hotel-and-government campaign ESET documented in 2019-2022 and revived in the US/Mexico in July 2024, and the Earth Estries Zingdoor/GhostSpider intrusions Trend Micro documented against government and NGO targets across Asia, Africa and Latin America in 2020-2024. In 2025-2026 the operation expanded further: joint attribution by Australia, Canada, the Czech Republic, Finland, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Poland, Spain, the UK and the US now covers more than 200 organisations across roughly 80 countries, including Viasat satellite infrastructure and Canadian telecom providers.

attribution.text: Attributed to the PRC Ministry of State Security by a 13-nation joint advisory led by CISA, FBI and NSA in August 2025 (AA25-239a), reinforced by named MSS contractor sanctions in 2025-2026 and by prior vendor attribution from Microsoft, Trend Micro, Kaspersky, Sygnia and Recorded Future.

name: FamousSparrow
description: Resurfaced in 2024 after inactivity. SparrowDoor backdoor, ShadowPad. ProxyLogon exploits. USA, Mexico, Honduras.

overview: FamousSparrow is a China-aligned cyber-espionage cluster first publicly documented by ESET in September 2021, best known for the custom SparrowDoor backdoor and a decade of intrusions against hotels, governments, engineering firms, law firms and international organizations across Europe, the Middle East, the Americas, Asia and Africa. ESET's original writeup traced the group's activity back to at least August 2019 and documented worldwide hospitality-sector victims plus government targets in a dozen countries including Brazil, Canada, France, Israel, Thailand and the United Kingdom.

In March 2025 ESET disclosed that FamousSparrow had re-emerged after roughly two years of silence, deploying two previously undocumented SparrowDoor variants (a modular plugin architecture compiled on 12 July 2024 and a second variant resembling what Trend Micro had called 'CrowDoor') against a US trade group in the financial sector and a Mexican research institute in July 2024, plus a Honduran governmental institution discovered while ESET was setting up victim tracking. The 2024 campaign was also the first observed instance of FamousSparrow deploying ShadowPad, side-loaded through the legitimate Microsoft Office IME executable imecmnt.exe and injected into wmplayer.exe; one SparrowDoor C&C server shared a TLS certificate fingerprint with known ShadowPad infrastructure.

MITRE ATT&CK canonicalised the cluster as part of Group G1045 (Salt Typhoon) in February 2025, and Microsoft's weather-themed China taxonomy also folds FamousSparrow into Salt Typhoon alongside GhostEmperor and Earth Estries. ESET, however, explicitly declines the merger: in the March 2025 writeup ESET states that FamousSparrow appears to be its own distinct cluster with only loose links to the others and that, absent technical justification, a shared third party such as a digital quartermaster better explains the tooling overlaps than a single actor. This ficha therefore records mitreId G1045 for interoperability while preserving the ESET-tracked cluster as a separate entry; see the ghostemperor / Salt Typhoon ficha for the consolidated MITRE view.

Initial-access tradecraft has been consistent across both epochs: exploitation of publicly-facing Microsoft Exchange (ProxyLogon in March 2021), Microsoft SharePoint and Oracle Opera, and in the 2024 campaign outdated Windows Server and Exchange builds compromised via publicly available exploits. SparrowDoor is dropped through DLL search-order hijacking abusing legitimate signed binaries (K7 Computing components in 2021; imecmnt.exe in 2024), executes without PE headers, uses XOR-encrypted configuration and C2, and supports interactive reverse shells, file transfer, process injection and token manipulation. The 2024 modular variant added parallelised execution of long-running commands so operators can run file I/O and interactive shells concurrently against the same host.

attribution.text: China-aligned by ESET (2021, 2025) and by Trend Micro's Earth Estries reporting; folded into the Salt Typhoon / MSS attribution by MITRE (G1045, Feb 2025), the joint 13-nation advisory AA25-239a (Aug 2025) and Microsoft's Salt Typhoon profile. ESET maintains FamousSparrow as a distinct cluster and has not itself endorsed the Salt Typhoon merger, citing lack of technical overlap sufficient to justify unification.

name: Rocke
description: Monero cryptojacking on Linux servers. Disables cloud security (Alibaba, Tencent). Cron persistence.

overview: Rocke is a Chinese-speaking cryptojacking crew first publicly named by Cisco Talos in August 2018, in the report 'Rocke: The Champion of Monero Miners'. The name comes from an email address (rocke@live.cn) tied to the Gitee and GitHub accounts hosting the actor's tooling. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the cluster as G0106; Malpedia catalogues it under the slug 'rocke'. Vendor coverage over 2018-2021 by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, Anomali Labs, Cisco Talos and independent security press established the group as one of the earliest and most technically distinctive server-side Monero-mining threat actors.

Rocke's mandate is purely financial: illicit Monero (XMR) mining on internet-exposed Linux servers, containers and public-cloud IaaS. Targeting is opportunistic rather than victim-driven; the group has weaponised n-day exploits for Apache Struts (CVE-2017-5638, CVE-2018-11776), Oracle WebLogic (CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2019-2725), Adobe ColdFusion (CVE-2018-15961), Apache ActiveMQ, Redis, Elasticsearch, Jenkins and, later, Atlassian Confluence to acquire cheap compute. Alibaba Cloud and Tencent Cloud tenants have been a recurring hunting ground.

The tradecraft that made Rocke a canonical case study is its ability to disable cloud-native security agents rather than merely evade them: Unit 42's January 2019 disclosure documented the actor uninstalling the Alibaba Cloud Aegis / aliyun agent and Tencent Cloud YunJing / qcloud-monitor before dropping XMRig-based miners, cron persistence, systemd services and shell init hooks. The 2021 Pro-Ocean evolution added an LD_PRELOAD userland rootkit to hide the miner process. Related tooling includes the Godlua Lua-based backdoor, the Watchbog cryptojacking framework, the Systemten dropper and a Go-language malware family disclosed by Anomali in September 2019.

Command-and-control infrastructure has moved with defender pressure: early campaigns used Pastebin and Chinese code-hosting sites (Gitee, GitHub) as dead-drop resolvers for miner configuration; by mid-2019 the group had shifted to CloudFront and Cloudflare Workers domain fronting (documented in Unit 42's 'Rocke'in the NetFlow' and 'Cloudy with a Chance of Entropy' posts), and later to Tor .onion services once the major CDNs cracked down on domain-fronting abuse. Attribution to a Chinese-speaking, criminally-motivated (not state-sponsored) crew rests on Chinese-language code comments, Chinese hosting choices, and shared code lineage with the 'Iron Cybercrime Group' cluster.

attribution.text: Attributed to a Chinese-speaking, financially-motivated criminal crew focused on illicit Monero mining. MITRE ATT&CK, Cisco Talos, Palo Alto Unit 42 and Anomali Labs all point to Chinese-language operators; the group shares code and infrastructure fingerprints with the 'Iron Cybercrime Group' cluster and hosts implants on Chinese code-sharing services (Gitee, gitcode). No US or allied government advisory or indictment has been issued for Rocke — attribution is technical / vendor consensus, not sovereign.

origin.text: First publicly disclosed by Cisco Talos on 30 August 2018; Talos and Unit 42 both trace observed campaigns to at least April 2018, when the actor began weaponising the Apache Struts, Oracle WebLogic and Adobe ColdFusion n-days that would become its trademark. MITRE ATT&CK dates the group's initial listed activity to 2018. Vendor reporting on the adjacent 'Iron Cybercrime Group' cluster extends the tooling lineage into 2016-2017.

mandate.text: Financial: unauthorised Monero mining at scale on hijacked Linux servers and public-cloud workloads. Rocke has no espionage, destructive or ransomware mandate in the classical sense (the Xbash worm's ransomware module targeted databases opportunistically and never decrypted on payment). The group's operational goal is to maximise sustained CPU-hours on compromised hosts, which shapes every tradecraft choice: killing rival miners, uninstalling cloud EDR/AV agents, hiding the miner process with LD_PRELOAD, and using CDN domain-fronting to keep the pool-facing C2 alive.

name: UNC3886
description: Active attack on Singapore 2025. Zero-days in Fortinet, VMware, Juniper. MOPSLED, RIFLESPINE, REPTILE malware.

overview: UNC3886 is a China-nexus cyber-espionage cluster tracked by Google Cloud's Mandiant since a September 2022 investigation exposed the first known abuse of malicious vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) to persist inside VMware ESXi hypervisors. Subsequent Mandiant reporting has documented the same operator across an unusually broad set of edge-and-virtualisation targets: FortiGate SSL-VPN appliances (CVE-2022-42475, BOLDMOVE), FortiManager/FortiAnalyzer with the FortiOS zero-day CVE-2022-41328, VMware vCenter (CVE-2023-34048), VMware Tools (CVE-2023-20867), and Juniper Networks MX routers running end-of-life Junos OS (CVE-2025-21590). MITRE has not yet published a Group ID for the cluster.

Attribution is expressed by Mandiant as a suspected China-nexus espionage actor, an assessment Sygnia's July 2025 Fire Ant report echoes on the basis of shared VIRTUALPITA binaries, exploitation of CVE-2023-34048 and CVE-2023-20867, and telecom-sector targeting. The most explicit public attribution to date came on 18 July 2025, when Singapore's Coordinating Minister for National Security K. Shanmugam publicly named UNC3886 as the group behind sustained attacks on the country's critical information infrastructure — the first time a national government singled out the cluster by name.

UNC3886's tradecraft is designed for edge devices and hypervisors, i.e. systems where endpoint-detection agents do not run. The group chains zero-day and n-day exploitation with hands-on-keyboard persistence: malicious VIBs and modified startup scripts on ESXi; kernel rootkits (REPTILE) and dynamic-linker hijacks (MEDUSA/SEAELF) on Linux vCenter and jump hosts; backdoored /usr/bin/ssh and /usr/sbin/sshd for credential capture; VMCI-socket backdoors (VIRTUALPITA, VIRTUALPIE, VIRTUALSHINE) that bypass network monitoring by living inside the hypervisor bus; and, on Juniper MX routers, six TinyShell-derived implants (appid, to, irad, lmpad, jdosd, oemd) that mimic legitimate Junos daemons and defeat Veriexec through /proc/pid/mem process injection.

Command-and-control is deliberately mundane: dead-drop URLs on GitHub Pages (MOPSLED), Google Drive with AES-CBC-wrapped payloads and MAC-address filename tokens (RIFLESPINE), Cloudflare-fronted HTTPS, and — on Juniper routers — a GOBRAT-style operational relay box (ORB) network of compromised SOHO devices reached over SSH. The overall pattern is long-dwell strategic espionage against defence, government, technology, telecoms, aerospace and energy targets across North America, Southeast Asia, Oceania, Europe and Africa, with no observable financial motivation.

attribution.text: Mandiant attributes UNC3886 as a suspected China-nexus cyber-espionage cluster across seven public reports (2022-2025). Sygnia's July 2025 Fire Ant investigation identifies a strong technical overlap (VIRTUALPITA binaries, identical CVE targeting) but explicitly refrains from conclusive attribution. Singapore's Coordinating Minister for National Security K. Shanmugam publicly named UNC3886 as a state-linked threat to the country's critical information infrastructure on 18 July 2025, the first government-level naming of the cluster.

name: Aquatic Panda
description: Operation FishMedley: 10 months, 7 organizations. ShadowPad, SodaMaster, RPipeCommander. Taiwan, Hungary, Turkey.

overview: Aquatic Panda is a China-nexus cyber-espionage cluster tracked by MITRE ATT&CK as G0143 and cross-referenced across the vendor community as Charcoal Typhoon (Microsoft), RedHotel (Recorded Future Insikt Group), TAG-22 (an earlier Recorded Future designation), Bronze University (Secureworks / now Sophos CTU), CHROMIUM (Microsoft's legacy chemical taxonomy) and ControlX. CrowdStrike's OverWatch team introduced the Aquatic Panda name publicly on December 29, 2021, after catching the group mid-intrusion at a large academic institution: the operator was probing a vulnerable VMware Horizon Tomcat process with a preconfigured JNDI-Injection-Exploit-1.0.jar targeting Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228), then attempted LSASS credential dumping with native rdrleakdiag.exe and cdump.exe before OverWatch cut the intrusion.

The remit is dual per CrowdStrike: intelligence collection aligned with PRC tasking and industrial espionage against targets whose intellectual property serves Chinese state priorities. Documented victimology spans telecommunications carriers (Nepal Telecom, the Philippine Department of Information and Communications Technology, Taiwan's Industrial Technology Research Institute), government agencies, universities and research institutes across South and Southeast Asia, Catholic charities and Asia-focused NGOs, geopolitical think tanks, aerospace and R&D companies, plus at least 17 countries reaching into Europe and North America per Recorded Future's RedHotel report of August 2023. Operational infrastructure has been traced to Chengdu, aligning with I-SOON's registered address.

Tooling is typical of the Winnti-adjacent Chinese contractor scene: ShadowPad and Cobalt Strike as workhorse implants, Winnti for Windows (MITRE S0141) and Winnti for Linux (S0430) for long-term persistence, PlugX and FunnySwitch, the Spyder modular backdoor (documented by Dr.Web in 2021), Brute Ratel C4 in later RedHotel intrusions, SodaMaster and the previously undocumented RPipeCommander in the FishMedley cluster, plus commodity RATs (njRAT, MITRE S0385) and living-off-the-land binaries (wevtutil, rundll32.exe, WinRAR and 7zip for staging). Initial access mixes vulnerable public-facing appliances (Log4Shell against VMware Horizon; GlassFish server exploitation; ProxyLogon-style Exchange bugs) with valid stolen credentials for lateral SSH and RDP movement, and a RestrictedAdmin registry edit to enable pass-the-hash over RDP.

On March 5, 2025 the US Department of Justice unsealed a Southern District of New York indictment against ten Chinese nationals - eight I-SOON (Anxun Information Technology Co., Ltd.) employees and two officers of China's Ministry of Public Security - for computer intrusions from 2016 to 2023 against US religious organisations, journalists, government agencies and foreign ministries. The FBI added the defendants to its cyber most-wanted list under the 'Aquatic Panda Cyber Threat Actors' heading, and ESET's Operation FishMedley writeup two weeks later independently corroborated I-SOON as the operator behind the 2022 campaign. CrowdStrike's 2025 Global Threat Report (published February 27, 2025) subsequently flagged a 150 percent year-over-year rise in China-nexus intrusions in 2024, with critical verticals up to 300 percent and expanded telecom targeting explicitly called out.

attribution.text: China-nexus, high confidence. MITRE ATT&CK describes G0143 as 'suspected China-based with a dual mission of intelligence collection and industrial espionage'; CrowdStrike, Microsoft, Recorded Future and Secureworks converge on a China-linked contractor cluster with Chengdu-based infrastructure. On March 5, 2025 the US DoJ unsealed indictments naming eight employees of the Chengdu contractor I-SOON (Anxun Information Technology Co., Ltd.) and two officers of China's Ministry of Public Security, and ESET's Operation FishMedley writeup independently confirmed I-SOON as the operational team behind the group's 2022 campaign.

origin.text: MITRE ATT&CK dates observed activity to at least May 2020, and CrowdStrike's adversary hub uses the same May 2020 start. Recorded Future's July 2021 TAG-22 writeup places intrusions against Nepal Telecom, Taiwan's ITRI and the Philippine DICT from mid-2020 onward; the August 2023 RedHotel writeup extends observed activity back to at least 2019. The DoJ indictment charges I-SOON intrusions spanning 2016 to 2023, and ESET's FishMedley writeup notes I-SOON operations dating to 2016, so the pre-2020 tradecraft was likely tracked by other vendors under different aliases before the AQUATIC PANDA name was coined.

notableOperations.summary: Recorded Future's Insikt Group documented a China-linked cluster it named TAG-22 targeting Nepal Telecom, Taiwan's Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) and the Philippine Department of Information and Communications Technology, plus Hong Kong universities. Initial access via GlassFish server exploitation; Cobalt Strike, ShadowPad, Winnti and Spyder used for persistence; Fishmaster Cobalt Strike loaders and Acunetix scanning. The report is the first public naming of infrastructure later mapped to Aquatic Panda / RedHotel.

notableOperations.name: Winnti for Linux SSH intrusions and second-round Windows access
notableOperations.summary: CrowdStrike's 2022 Falcon OverWatch Threat Hunting Report documented Aquatic Panda operations against Linux fleets: valid stolen credentials over SSH to reach victim hosts, malicious shell scripts to stage Linux Winnti (MITRE S0430), ld.so preload persistence, and command-history clearing to evade defence. On Windows, the operator loaded a malicious DLL into the legitimate SecurityHealthService.exe, used wevtutil to dump security event logs, cleared Windows Event Logs, edited the registry to enable RestrictedAdmin (pass-the-hash over RDP), and used WMI for lateral movement.

notableOperations.name: RedHotel global 17-country espionage campaign
notableOperations.summary: Recorded Future's August 2023 RedHotel writeup consolidated three years of intrusions across 17 countries in Asia, Europe and North America, targeting academia, aerospace, government, media, telecommunications, R&D companies, COVID-19 research organisations and online gambling operations. Infrastructure administration traced to Chengdu. Tooling: Cobalt Strike, Brute Ratel C4, Winnti, ShadowPad, FunnySwitch, Spyder, web shells, GlassFish exploitation, Acunetix scanning. Recorded Future explicitly cross-references AQUATIC PANDA and TAG-22 as aliases.

notableOperations.name: Operation FishMedley: 10-month, 7-organisation espionage campaign
notableOperations.summary: ESET's March 2025 Operation FishMedley writeup documented a global espionage operation spanning January to October 2022 that compromised seven high-value targets across Taiwan, Hungary, Turkey, Thailand, the United States and France: two governmental organisations, two Catholic charities, an NGO focused on Asia, a geopolitical think tank and one unattributed victim. ShadowPad (packed with ScatterBee), SodaMaster and the previously undocumented RPipeCommander were staged alongside the Spyder modular backdoor first analysed by Dr.Web in 2021. ESET explicitly lists Aquatic Panda, TAG-22, Earth Lusca and Red Dev 10 as aliases for the FishMonger cluster it attributes to I-SOON.

notableOperations.name: Charcoal Typhoon abuse of OpenAI large language models
notableOperations.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence and OpenAI disclosed on February 14, 2024 that five state-affiliated groups, including Charcoal Typhoon (the Microsoft designation for Aquatic Panda), had used ChatGPT accounts for early-stage tasks - reconnaissance of Microsoft/telecom victims, translation of technical documents, drafting phishing content and troubleshooting scripts. Accounts were terminated. The disclosure was the first public evidence of Aquatic Panda operators incorporating commercial LLMs into their workflow.

notableOperations.name: US DoJ indictment of I-SOON and MPS officers; FBI Aquatic Panda most-wanted listing
notableOperations.summary: On March 5, 2025 the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York unsealed indictments against ten Chinese nationals: eight I-SOON (Anxun Information Technology Co., Ltd., Chengdu) employees including CEO Wu Haibo and COO Chen Cheng, plus two officers of China's Ministry of Public Security (Wang Liyu, Sheng Jing). Charges cover computer intrusions from 2016 to 2023 against US religious organisations, journalists, government agencies and foreign ministries. I-SOON was paid USD 10,000-75,000 per compromised inbox and sold stolen data to 43 Chinese government bureaus. The FBI simultaneously added the defendants to its cyber most-wanted list under the 'Aquatic Panda Cyber Threat Actors' banner.
