name: APT37
description: Operation HanKook Phantom 2025. ROKRAT, BabyShark, Dolphin backdoor. Cloud persistence, trojanized software.

overview: APT37 is a North Korean state-sponsored cyber-espionage group active since at least 2012, tracked by MITRE ATT&CK as G0067 and by the wider vendor community under a long list of cryptonyms: Reaper (FireEye/Mandiant), ScarCruft (Kaspersky), Group123 (Cisco Talos), Ricochet Chollima (CrowdStrike), InkySquid (Volexity), Red Eyes and Venus 121 (Korean CERT/vendors). Public reporting attributes the group to the Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB), North Korea's principal foreign-intelligence service.

Unlike Lazarus and its sub-clusters, APT37 has no meaningful financial-crime mandate. Its remit is strategic espionage aligned to DPRK regime priorities, with a strong bias toward South Korean and diaspora targets: North Korean defectors and human-rights activists, journalists covering the peninsula (notably the Daily NK site targeted in the 2021 InkySquid IE/Edge chain), academics and think-tank researchers, government and defence entities, and â since 2017 â episodic collection against Japan, Vietnam, the Middle East and Russian defence contractors.

The group's technical trademark is the persistent use of Korean-language document lures (HWP Hangul Word Processor files, LNK shortcuts and CHM help files), a family of custom implants built around ROKRAT (aka DOGCALL) and its successors CoralDeck, HAPPYWORK, POORAIM, WINERACK, BLUELIGHT, Chinotto, Dolphin, M2RAT and NarwhalRAT, and a marked appetite for zero-days: Adobe Flash CVE-2016-4171 (Operation Daybreak) and CVE-2018-4878, IE/Edge chains used against Daily NK in 2021, and Windows MSHTML CVE-2024-38178 (Operation Code on Toast). Command-and-control almost always rides on legitimate cloud services â Dropbox, pCloud, Yandex Disk, Box, Google Cloud, Cloudflare Workers and, in 2023, Ably real-time messaging â a pattern documented across every major vendor report from 2016 onwards.

attribution.text: Attributed to North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB) by FireEye/Mandiant, Kaspersky, Cisco Talos, ESET, Volexity, CrowdStrike and MITRE ATT&CK. No US DoJ indictment or CISA advisory names APT37 specifically (unlike Lazarus/APT38); attribution rests on vendor tradecraft, infrastructure and code overlap analysis reinforced by South Korean government (KISA/NIS) reporting.

origin.text: First observed activity dates to 2012 per MITRE ATT&CK, with FireEye/Mandiant's 2018 profile placing early operations against South Korean targets in that same window. Cisco Talos's Group 123 series (April 2017 to May 2018) documents the group's initial ROKRAT development, and Kaspersky's Operation Daybreak write-up shows the group already burning an Adobe Flash zero-day (CVE-2016-4171) by mid-2016.

No financial-crime remit â that role is filled inside the RGB by Lazarus and its Bluenoroff/Andariel/APT38 subclusters.

name: APT1
description: Based in Shanghai, Pudong. 140+ intrusions 2006-2010. 5 officers indicted by DOJ USA. Legacy persists.

overview: APT1 is the Chinese state-sponsored cyber-espionage group publicly exposed in February 2013 by Mandiant as the People's Liberation Army General Staff Department's 3rd Department, 2nd Bureau, Military Unit Cover Designator 61398 — the branch known outside China as PLA Unit 61398. Mandiant documented 141 confirmed intrusions against organisations in 20 major industry verticals, with the majority in English-speaking countries, over a period beginning in 2006 and running through the report's publication.

The group is one of the earliest APT clusters to be given a public numeric designation, and MITRE tracks it as G0006 with the aliases Comment Crew, Comment Group, Byzantine Candor and Shanghai Group. The 'Comment Crew' name comes from the operators' habit of hiding command instructions inside HTML comment tags on legitimate websites, an early living-off-the-land pattern.

On 19 May 2014 the US Department of Justice unsealed an indictment against five PLA Unit 61398 officers — Wang Dong ('UglyGorilla'), Sun Kailiang ('Jack Sun'), Wen Xinyu ('WinXYHappy'), Huang Zhenyu ('hzy_lhx') and Gu Chunhui ('KandyGoo') — for economic espionage against Westinghouse, US Steel, Alcoa, Allegheny Technologies, SolarWorld and the United Steelworkers union. This was the first time the US government publicly charged uniformed foreign military officers with cyber crimes.

Public activity attributed to this specific tooling and infrastructure cluster largely stopped after the Mandiant report. Operators, tradecraft and target sets are widely assessed to have been redistributed across the PRC's newer MSS-run APT clusters, and APT1's tools, target list and public exposure remain the canonical baseline every subsequent China-nexus writeup measures itself against.

attribution.text: Attributed to the 2nd Bureau of the People's Liberation Army General Staff Department 3rd Department, Military Unit Cover Designator 61398, based at 208 Datong Road in the Pudong New Area of Shanghai. Attribution was first published by Mandiant (Feb 2013), formalised by the US Department of Justice indictment of five named PLA officers (May 2014), catalogued by MITRE ATT&CK as G0006, and reinforced by CrowdStrike (Comment Panda) and Malpedia.

origin.text: Mandiant's 2013 report placed first observed intrusion activity in 2006, with 141 organisations compromised through late 2012. MITRE's canonical G0006 entry likewise dates the group to 2006. CrowdStrike had tracked the same cluster internally as Comment Panda from at least 2011, and infrastructure re-use (WEBC2, BISCUIT) is documented back to 2006 in the Mandiant appendices.

name: Bitter
description: Targeting Bangladesh, Pakistan, China, Saudi Arabia. BitterRAT, ArtraDownloader, AndroRAT malware.

overview: BITTER (MITRE G1002; also tracked as T-APT-17, APT-C-08 and TA397) is a South-Asia-nexus cyber-espionage cluster that has been active since at least November 2013, when Forcepoint's X-Labs first documented targeted spearphishing against Pakistani government users. Over more than a decade the operator has progressively broadened its target set to include China, Bangladesh, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, while retaining a signature tradecraft of scheduled-task-based staging and a compact family of custom Windows and Android implants.

Attribution is unusually consistent across independent vendors: Proofpoint's 2025 'Bitter End' retrospective assesses the operator as highly likely aligned with an Indian state interest, Kaspersky's SecureList quarterly reports describe it as a South-Asian espionage cluster, and Proofpoint's 2024 TA397 disclosure notes that operational activity falls almost entirely within the UTC+5:30 working window. MITRE's canonical group page lists Pakistan, China, Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia as primary target countries, a mix that aligns with an Indian foreign-intelligence collection remit rather than any other South-Asian sponsor.

The operator's malware arsenal has evolved but stayed compact and recognisable: the original BitterRAT and ArtraDownloader Windows implants from the 2013-2020 campaigns; ZxxZ, disclosed by Cisco Talos in 2022 alongside a shift toward Bangladeshi military targets; the ORPCBackdoor and MuuyDownloader pair used against Chinese government, nuclear-energy and aerospace organisations from 2021 onward; and the newer WmRAT and MiyaRAT backdoors that Proofpoint attributed to TA397 in its December 2024 writeup on Turkish defense-sector intrusions. On mobile, BITTER has fielded AndroRAT variants disguised as Islamic-prayer and Kashmir news apps and, per Cyble, the Dracarys spyware built into a trojanised Signal clone.

Tradecraft is spearphishing-heavy and rarely bothers with zero-days: weaponised Office and RTF documents (historically CVE-2012-0158, later CVE-2018-0798 and the Equation Editor family), RAR archives that abuse alternate data streams to hide LNK payloads, and scheduled tasks that beacon out to staging domains registered on Namecheap or GoDaddy with Let's Encrypt certificates. The one significant deviation is CVE-2021-1732, a Windows Win32k elevation-of-privilege zero-day that DBAppSecurity attributed to BITTER in February 2021 and Microsoft patched the same month.

attribution.text: Assessed with medium-to-high confidence by multiple independent vendors as a South-Asia-nexus espionage operator most likely aligned with Indian state interests. Proofpoint's June 2025 retrospective explicitly assesses TA397 as 'highly likely' India-backed based on eight years of victimology, tradecraft and time-of-day analysis. Kaspersky's SecureList quarterly reports and Cisco Talos both describe the actor as South-Asian; MITRE does not publish a sponsoring country. No government has issued a formal indictment.

name: APT36
description: Massive targeting of India. DeskRAT Golang, CapraRAT Android, Crimson RAT. Cross-platform (Linux MayaOS).

overview: APT36 — most commonly known in vendor reporting as Transparent Tribe — is a Pakistan-nexus cyber-espionage group active since at least 2013. Its targeting is unusually consistent for a decade-old cluster: Indian military and paramilitary personnel, the Ministry of Defence and its procurement chain, diplomatic missions, and Indian and Afghan academic institutions. Public reporting also uses the aliases Mythic Leopard (CrowdStrike), ProjectM (Unit 42), COPPER FIELDSTONE (Secureworks) and Operation C-Major, the name Proofpoint gave to the 2016 operation that first exposed the group's Crimson RAT toolset.

The tradecraft baseline is spearphishing with weaponised Microsoft Office documents that abuse well-worn Equation Editor and OLE bugs — CVE-2012-0158, CVE-2015-1641 and CVE-2017-11882 — to drop Crimson RAT and its lighter cousins Peppy RAT and ObliqueRAT. Where the group stands out is in its mobile operations: it has run one of the longest-lived Android surveillanceware campaigns of any known state-aligned actor, from the AhMyth-derived Android trojans documented by Kaspersky in 2020, through the CapraRAT builds that ESET, Amnesty and SentinelLabs have tracked from 2020 to 2024, and into the fake Signal, Telegram and YouTube apps that carried CapraRAT to targeted victims via romance and honey-trap lures.

Attribution to a specific service inside Pakistan has never been formally established by a Western government. What exists is repeated OSINT convergence: Unit 42's 2016 ProjectM research pinned domain registrations to a Karachi-based individual whose name later appeared in Crimson RAT debug symbols; Secureworks catalogues the cluster as COPPER FIELDSTONE and describes it as fulfilling Pakistani strategic intelligence collection requirements; Amnesty International's 2020 investigation into a Facebook honey-trap network against Indian Army officers linked the C2 infrastructure directly to Transparent Tribe. Indian vendors — SEQRITE, K7, CYFIRMA — with the deepest visibility into the target set consistently place the group as Pakistan-aligned.

The 2023-2026 arc has been one of platform diversification more than sophistication uplift. Zscaler documented the ElizaRAT .NET implant using Telegram as C2 against Indian government targets in September 2023. In August 2025 the same cluster began abusing Linux .desktop files as droppers against Indian defence users of BOSS Linux and Zorin OS, and in August 2026 Acronis tied Transparent Tribe to PATCHCORD, a Google Sheets-driven backdoor deployed against Afghan telecom infrastructure through fake VPN apps. The through-line across all of it is opportunistic decoy engineering: Kavach MFA installers, Aarogya Setu COVID trackers, Pahalgam terror-attack briefings, Rafale procurement documents — whatever an Indian military or civil-service reader is most likely to open the week the operators send it.

attribution.text: Pakistan-nexus, assessed by multiple vendors as fulfilling Pakistani strategic intelligence collection requirements. No Western government has issued a formal attribution to a specific Pakistani service; the strongest public evidence is Unit 42's 2016 ProjectM OSINT tying domain registrations and Crimson RAT debug artefacts to a Karachi-based operator. Consistent placement as Pakistan-linked across CrowdStrike, Secureworks, Kaspersky, ESET, Cisco Talos, Zscaler, SentinelLabs, Amnesty International and Indian vendors (SEQRITE, K7, CYFIRMA).

name: APT12
description: Targeting Taiwan government networks 2025. IXESHE malware, web-based CNACOM campaign. Consistent with PRC goals.

overview: APT12 - also tracked as Numbered Panda, IXESHE, DynCalc, DNSCalc, Calc Team and TG-2754 - is a China-nexus cyber-espionage cluster first documented publicly by Trend Micro in a 2012 whitepaper ("IXESHE: An APT Campaign"), with earliest observed activity going back to 2009. The group targets governments, defence contractors, media outlets, high-tech firms and electronics manufacturers, with a persistent East-Asian focus on Taiwan and Japan and repeated campaigns against diplomatic missions and Tibetan / Uyghur diaspora organisations.

The group entered mainstream awareness in January 2013 when the New York Times disclosed - drawing on Mandiant's incident-response findings - that Chinese attackers had spent four months inside its network stealing corporate passwords and monitoring reporters covering the family wealth of then Premier Wen Jiabao. Mandiant tied the intrusion to a distinct actor separate from APT1 and later, in FireEye reporting, identified the responsible cluster as APT12. Within months of the NYT disclosure APT12 rotated its toolset - retiring backdoors that had been burned in Mandiant's public reporting and rolling out RIPTIDE, HIGHTIDE, THREEBYTE and WATERSPOUT - a rare public example of a Chinese actor visibly re-tooling in response to attribution.

APT12's signature tradecraft is spearphishing with weaponised Microsoft Office documents (heavily CVE-2012-0158, alongside CVE-2011-0611 and CVE-2012-1889) that drop the IXESHE and later Etumbot backdoors, coupled with strategic web compromises (the 2015 CNACOM campaign against a Taiwan-related news site). Command-and-control uses HTTP with base64-encoded parameters, RC4 payload encryption, and a distinctive technique - the group's DynCalc / DNSCalc alias - of encoding C2 IP addresses inside DNS TXT / A-record responses so operators can rotate infrastructure without new droppers being pushed to victims.

Public attribution to a specific Chinese state entity has never been formalised in an indictment. MITRE's G0005 entry places APT12 as "a threat group that has been attributed to China" without naming a sponsoring service, and FireEye / Mandiant have consistently described the group as PRC state-linked based on target selection (Taiwan defence policy, Japanese defence, diaspora, Western media reporting on Chinese leadership) and operational tempo. The CFR Cyber Operations Tracker likewise attributes APT12 to the People's Republic of China without naming a specific unit. No new significant APT12-branded campaigns have been publicly disclosed by FireEye / Mandiant since the mid-2010s, though independent trackers continue to see IXESHE-family activity against Taiwan.

attribution.text: China-nexus state-sponsored espionage cluster. FireEye / Mandiant, MITRE ATT&CK and the CFR Cyber Operations Tracker all attribute APT12 to the People's Republic of China based on target selection (Taiwan, Japan, Tibetan / Uyghur diaspora, Western media covering Chinese leadership) and tradecraft overlap. No US, Taiwanese or Japanese indictment has publicly named a specific PLA or MSS unit, so vendor descriptions such as "PLA-linked" remain inferences from targeting and infrastructure, not government attributions.
attribution.note: China attribution is canonical (MITRE + Mandiant + CFR); the specific service - PLA vs MSS - is not publicly established.

origin.text: Earliest observed activity is 2009, when Trend Micro began tracking the IXESHE backdoor family in intrusions against East Asian governments, Taiwanese electronics firms and a German telecommunications company. The APT12 designation itself was popularised by Mandiant / FireEye after the January 2013 New York Times disclosure. MITRE ATT&CK's G0005 entry cites first-seen activity in 2009.

mandate.text: Long-dwell intelligence collection aligned with PRC political, military and economic priorities: monitoring of Taiwan and Japanese government / defence, of Western media outlets reporting on Chinese leadership (New York Times 2012), and of Tibetan and Uyghur diaspora organisations. Post-NYT tooling changes (RIPTIDE / HIGHTIDE / WATERSPOUT rollout) indicate the group treats operator infrastructure and backdoors as expendable so long as access to strategic target sets is preserved.

techniques.usage: IXESHE payloads and C2 traffic are RC4-encrypted and base64-encoded; Etumbot decodes its C2 URLs at runtime from an on-disk configuration blob.

techniques.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
techniques.usage: Etumbot decodes RC4-encrypted, base64-wrapped C2 responses at runtime; HIGHTIDE / THREEBYTE / WATERSPOUT similarly decode base64-wrapped C2 payloads before execution.

techniques.name: Process Discovery
techniques.usage: IXESHE backdoor enumerates the process list on victim hosts to identify security software and running applications before staging further activity.

techniques.name: System Information Discovery
techniques.usage: Etumbot and IXESHE beacons include host information - OS version, hostname, username, ANSI codepage - in initial C2 registration to fingerprint victims.

techniques.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
techniques.usage: Etumbot queries the victim's HTTP proxy configuration via WinInet APIs so subsequent C2 traffic transparently traverses corporate proxies.

techniques.name: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
techniques.usage: All APT12 backdoor families - IXESHE, Etumbot, RIPTIDE, HIGHTIDE, THREEBYTE, WATERSPOUT - use HTTP GET / POST with distinctive User-Agent strings and URI patterns for C2.

techniques.name: Dynamic Resolution: Domain Generation Algorithms
techniques.usage: Signature DynCalc / DNSCalc technique - operators encode C2 IPv4 octets inside numeric fields of DNS answers so implants can compute their next callback address without a firmware update.

techniques.name: Data Encoding: Standard Encoding
techniques.usage: Etumbot, HIGHTIDE and WATERSPOUT base64-encode command output and file transfers inside HTTP request bodies and query strings to blend into web traffic.

techniques.name: Encrypted Channel: Symmetric Cryptography
techniques.usage: Etumbot wraps C2 message bodies in RC4 (keyed off the URI's session id) before base64 encoding, so recovered PCAPs decrypt only with the paired session key.

techniques.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
techniques.usage: IXESHE and Etumbot support operator commands to download and execute additional stagers, including credential-stealing and lateral-movement modules, over the same HTTP C2 channel.

techniques.name: Proxy: External Proxy
techniques.usage: Trend Micro documented APT12 using compromised victim boxes inside legitimate networks as HTTP relays for other IXESHE infections, so C2 traffic terminates on trusted-looking IP space.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
techniques.usage: Stolen credentials, mailbox contents and reconnaissance output are exfiltrated inside the same base64 / RC4 HTTP request bodies used for backdoor tasking - matching the NYT intrusion pattern where operators pulled password stores over months.

name: DoNot Team
description: Expanded to European foreign ministries 2025. LoptikMod, Tanzeem malware. Kashmir-focused. Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh.

overview: DoNot Team is an India-nexus cyber-espionage cluster active since at least 2016, first documented by NETSCOUT/ASERT in March 2018 under the name Donot Team and by Qihoo 360 shortly afterwards as APT-C-35. Other trackers use SectorE02 (NSHC ThreatRecon), Origami Elephant (Kaspersky), Viceroy Tiger (CrowdStrike) and Mint Tempest (Microsoft's 2023 weather-themed taxonomy). This ficha treats them as aliases for the same cluster.

The group's canonical Windows toolkit is the yty modular framework (also called Jaca in later Morphisec reporting), delivered by weaponised Microsoft Office documents that abuse the Equation Editor bug CVE-2017-11882 and the Office memory-corruption bug CVE-2018-0798 to fetch further stagers. ESET's January 2022 write-up traced two long-running yty branches — DarkMusical and Gedit — against South Asian militaries and embassies from 2020 into 2021, and Cisco Talos's October 2020 disclosure of Firestarter documented the group's parallel Android toolkit abusing Google Firebase Cloud Messaging for delivery and C2.

Public attribution places the group within India's intelligence ecosystem. Amnesty International's Security Lab investigation into a 2019-2020 targeting campaign against a Togolese human-rights defender identified overlap between DoNot Team infrastructure and Innefu Labs, an Indian surveillance-technology vendor that sells predictive-policing and biometric services to Indian law enforcement and armed forces. Innefu denied direct involvement; Amnesty stood by the linkage. This has since been treated by multiple vendors as the strongest public evidence of an India-nexus placement, without a formal government attribution comparable to those made against Chinese or Iranian clusters.

DoNot Team's mandate is regional-espionage: signals collection against Pakistan (military, intelligence and MFA), Kashmir separatist entities and diaspora, and neighbouring South Asian governments (Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, Maldives), with a widening interest in European foreign ministries and diplomatic personnel in the Middle East. Trellix reported a 2024 spear-phishing campaign against a Southern European government entity, and Kaspersky's Q1 2024 APT trends report catalogued continued Origami Elephant targeting of Ministry of Foreign Affairs staff.

attribution.text: Public reporting places the cluster in India's intelligence ecosystem. Amnesty International's Security Lab identified infrastructure overlap between DoNot Team spyware used against a Togolese activist and Innefu Labs, an Indian surveillance-vendor selling to Indian law enforcement. No government has formally indicted the operators; the placement rests on private-sector reporting.
attribution.note: No sovereign attribution comparable to US/UK statements against Chinese or Iranian clusters. Innefu Labs denied direct involvement.

name: APT5
description: Focus on telecom and satellite communications. NSA confirmed Citrix zero-day exploitation. Advanced networking device targeting.

overview: APT5 is a China-nexus cyber-espionage cluster tracked publicly since at least 2007 and one of the longest-running actors on the MITRE ATT&CK group list. MITRE's canonical listing is G1023 with the aliases Keyhole Panda (CrowdStrike), BRONZE FLEETWOOD (SecureWorks), MANGANESE (Microsoft's legacy chemical-element scheme, since renamed Mulberry Typhoon under the 2023 weather taxonomy), UNC2630 (Mandiant, for the 2020-2021 Pulse Secure sub-cluster) and Poisoned Flight (Mandiant's internal name for the 2010s tooling). Multiple vendors track those cryptonyms as the same activity cluster; this ficha follows the same convention.

Historical Mandiant reporting places APT5 activity as far back as 2007, with a marked bias toward US and allied defence, aerospace, satellite-communications, telecommunications and technology-industry targets. CrowdStrike's Keyhole Panda profile summarises the group as a China-nexus adversary focused on Western business interests, defence and manufacturing verticals, and Microsoft's Mulberry Typhoon writeup places the actor in the same target set. The group is consistently described as espionage-only; no public reporting attributes financially motivated intrusions to it.

Since 2019 APT5 has been one of the most aggressive Chinese actors in the edge-appliance exploitation space. Mandiant's 2021 "Check Your Pulse" report attributed a wave of Pulse Connect Secure VPN intrusions to UNC2630 (linked with high confidence to APT5), abusing CVE-2019-11510 (arbitrary file read) and the 2021 zero-day CVE-2021-22893 (authentication bypass) to drop a purpose-built web-shell family — SLIGHTPULSE, STEADYPULSE, RADIALPULSE, PULSECHECK, HARDPULSE, LOCKPICK, ATRIUM, THINBLOOD and BLOODMINE — that patched legitimate Pulse binaries in place to survive reboots and firmware upgrades. CISA published two joint advisories (AA20-107A, AA21-110A) covering the same intrusion set.

In December 2022 the NSA, CISA and FBI released a joint Cybersecurity Advisory pinning exploitation of the Citrix ADC / Citrix Gateway zero-day CVE-2022-27518 on APT5 by name — one of the rare occasions the US intelligence community has publicly attributed a live 0-day campaign to a specific Chinese cluster. Mandiant published a companion technical report the same day. The June 2022 CISA/NSA/FBI advisory AA22-158A ("PRC State-Sponsored Cyber Actors Exploit Network Providers and Devices") documents the broader pattern APT5 is a leading exemplar of: multi-year exploitation of unpatched CVEs on internet-exposed routers, VPN concentrators and application-delivery controllers to pivot into telecommunications and defence networks.

attribution.text: Attributed by multiple independent trackers to a China-nexus state-sponsored cluster. MITRE ATT&CK, Mandiant, CrowdStrike, Microsoft and the joint NSA/CISA/FBI December 2022 advisory all place APT5 in the PRC state-sponsored category; there is no unsealed US indictment naming individual operators as of September 2026, which distinguishes APT5 from APT31 or APT40.

name: BlackTech
description: Cisco router firmware modifications. PLEAD malware. Hot-patching firmware in memory. Targeting Japan and US via subsidiaries.

overview: BlackTech is a China-nexus cyber-espionage cluster that MITRE ATT&CK catalogues as G0098 and that has been continuously active against East Asian government, industrial, technology, media, electronics and telecommunications targets since at least 2010. The group is heavily aliased across the vendor space: Palmerworm (Symantec / Broadcom), T-APT-03 (Trend Micro's older cryptonym), Circuit Panda and Radio Panda (CrowdStrike), HUAPI (older CrowdStrike), Temp.Overboard (FireEye / Mandiant) and, since 2024, Earth Hundun (Trend Micro's current Earth-prefixed cryptonym). This ficha treats those labels as aliases for the same cluster.

Primary targeting is Japan, Taiwan and Hong Kong, with regular expansion into US and Japanese parent-company networks reached by pivoting through smaller Asian subsidiaries — a tradecraft pattern that the September 2023 joint advisory by the US NSA, CISA and FBI together with Japan's National Police Agency (NPA) and National center of Incident readiness and Strategy for Cybersecurity (NISC) singled out as the group's signature move. Sectorally, BlackTech has repeatedly hit government ministries, defence contractors, semiconductor and electronics manufacturers, telecom operators, media groups and industrial-technology firms.

The group's toolset is one of the widest in Chinese state-linked intrusion sets. PLEAD (backdoor and downloader) and TSCookie / TSC_QuaverUn (loader / RAT) are the long-running Windows implants documented by Trend Micro, JPCERT/CC and ESET since 2017-2018; a Linux port (ELF_PLEAD, ELF_TSCookie) followed in 2020. Waterbear and its 2024 successor Deuterbear, IconDown, Gh0stTimes and the FlagPro downloader — first tied to BlackTech by JPCERT/CC in 2021 — round out the Windows arsenal, while BendyBear, disclosed by Palo Alto Unit 42 in February 2021, is a heavily obfuscated stage-0 shellcode used to stage Waterbear on high-value targets. BlackTech has also been observed abusing stolen Taiwanese code-signing certificates (D-Link, Changing Information Technology) and, in the ASUS WebStorage incident of 2019, hijacking a legitimate software-update channel to push PLEAD.

The defining tradecraft, however, is compromise of Cisco IOS-based routers in victim networks — replacing router firmware with modified images that allow persistent, privileged access into internal networks and enable operators to pivot from trusted internal subsidiaries into the parent enterprise. The September 27, 2023 joint advisory AA23-270A (NSA/CISA/FBI/NPA/NISC) documented the technique in operational detail, including the use of a stolen Cisco Catalyst engineering command to disable logging, and Cisco Talos published a companion advisory the same day. BlackTech remains active into 2024 under Trend Micro's Earth Hundun cryptonym, with the Waterbear/Deuterbear evolution and continued targeting of the Asia-Pacific tech sector.

attribution.text: China-nexus, assessed with high confidence by MITRE ATT&CK, Trend Micro, Palo Alto Unit 42, Mandiant / Symantec, ESET and JPCERT/CC. The September 2023 joint advisory by NSA, CISA, FBI, Japan's NPA and NISC formally described BlackTech as 'People's Republic of China-linked cyber actors', the closest thing to a government attribution the group has received. No individual operators or MSS/PLA units have been publicly named in a US or Japanese indictment; vendor and community consensus is that BlackTech operates on behalf of PRC state interests.

name: Dragonfly
description: ICS/SCADA specialist. Havex malware supply chain attacks. Capable of disrupting US power grid. 84 countries affected.

overview: Dragonfly - also tracked as Energetic Bear, Crouching Yeti, Berserk Bear, IRON LIBERTY and TeamSpy - is a Russia-nexus cyber-espionage cluster that has targeted the energy sector and other critical-infrastructure verticals since at least 2010-2011. Symantec first documented the group in June 2014 (Dragonfly 1.0) and again in September 2017 (Dragonfly 2.0) after a resurgence targeting US and European energy operators. MITRE ATT&CK catalogues the cluster as G0035 and Malpedia mirrors it under the actor slug 'energetic_bear'.

On 24 March 2022 the US Department of Justice unsealed a 2021 grand-jury indictment in the District of Kansas charging three FSB officers - Pavel Aleksandrovich Akulov, Mikhail Mikhailovich Gavrilov and Marat Valeryevich Tyukov - who worked out of Military Unit 71330, better known as FSB Center 16, with running the Dragonfly 2.0 campaign between 2012 and 2017. The indictment describes the Havex supply-chain compromise of ICS vendor websites and the 2017 intrusion at the Wolf Creek Nuclear Operating Corporation in Burlington, Kansas. The FBI added the three officers to its Cyber Most Wanted list on the same day, and the US Department of State's Rewards for Justice programme offered up to USD 10 million for information leading to their identification or location.

Dragonfly's tradecraft blends three initial-access modes: spearphishing with malicious document attachments, strategic-web-compromise 'watering-hole' plants against energy-industry news sites and vendor portals, and trojanised ICS software installers (Havex was delivered inside legitimate installers pulled from the eWon/Talos2, MB Connect Line and MESA Imaging vendor sites). Post-exploitation the operators lean on Havex, Karagany (Xtunnel-like backdoor), Heriplor and Listrix - all four of which MITRE tracks as Dragonfly-exclusive families (S0093, S0094, S0376, S0381) - alongside PsExec, credential-dumping utilities and PowerShell for lateral movement inside OT-adjacent enterprise networks.

The group's post-2017 activity pivoted toward US state, local, tribal and territorial (SLTT) government targets alongside continued energy-sector interest: CISA/FBI advisory AA20-296A (20 October 2020, updated 22 October 2020) attributed a wave of scanning and successful compromises of SLTT networks in the run-up to the 2020 US election to the Berserk Bear/Energetic Bear cluster. Public reporting after the March 2022 DoJ unsealing was thin; the group appears to have continued lower-tempo operations, and Cyllex has not observed material new Dragonfly-attributed tradecraft in the 2023-2025 window beyond the campaigns already covered by CISA and Symantec.

attribution.text: Attributed to the Russian FSB (Federal Security Service), specifically Military Unit 71330 - FSB Center 16, the FSB's SIGINT and computer-network-operations arm. The US Department of Justice's 26 August 2021 indictment (unsealed 24 March 2022) named three Center 16 officers - Pavel Akulov, Mikhail Gavrilov and Marat Tyukov - as the operators behind the 2012-2017 Havex/Dragonfly 2.0 campaign. The US Department of the Treasury's OFAC has separately designated Center 16 personnel for related activity, and CISA advisories TA18-074A and AA20-296A attribute the campaign to 'Russian government cyber actors'.

mandate.text: Long-dwell intrusion access into industrial control system (ICS) and energy-sector networks in NATO countries, with a persistent focus on electric utilities, oil & gas, nuclear power, water and, more recently, US state and local government. name: APT40
description: Naval modernization support. Maritime technology theft. Port authorities in Malaysia, ASEAN. SSF, web shells, credential dumping.

overview: APT40 is a People's Republic of China state-sponsored cyber-espionage group formally attributed by the US Department of Justice to the Ministry of State Security's Hainan State Security Department (HSSD), operating in practice through a front company named Hainan Xiandun Technology Development Company based in Haikou, Hainan Province. The July 2021 unsealed indictment named four defendants: three HSSD intelligence officers (Ding Xiaoyang, Cheng Qingmin, Zhu Yunmin) and one Hainan Xiandun contractor (Wu Shurong), and set out a 2011-2018 conspiracy that stole terabytes of trade secrets, research and government data across at least a dozen countries.

The cluster is one of the most heavily aliased Chinese actors in threat intelligence. MITRE's canonical listing is APT40 (G0065) with the aliases TEMP.Periscope, TEMP.Jumper, Leviathan (Proofpoint), BRONZE MOHAWK (SecureWorks), Kryptonite Panda (CrowdStrike), MUDCARP (Cisco Talos / Accenture iDefense), ISLANDDREAMS and, more recently, GINGHAM TYPHOON (Microsoft, under its 2023 weather-themed taxonomy). Multiple vendors track the group under those separate cryptonyms; this ficha treats them as aliases for the same cluster.

APT40's mandate is dual-purpose: strategic intelligence collection for the MSS and industrial-espionage support for the PRC's naval modernisation programme, with a marked bias toward maritime, naval-defence, shipping and port-authority targets, marine engineering and underwater-warfare research, and the universities that feed those supply chains. Historical Mandiant reporting placed early activity as far back as 2009, with sustained targeting of the US, UK, EU, Cambodia, Malaysia, Norway, Saudi Arabia, Switzerland and the UAE.

Since 2020 the group has been a leading proponent of edge-appliance and public-facing application exploitation: it participated in the follow-on ProxyLogon (Microsoft Exchange) mass-exploitation wave in March 2021, and the joint eight-agency advisory AA24-190A published by ASD's ACSC with CISA/FBI/NSA/NCSC-UK/CCCS/NCSC-NZ/BfV/KISA/NISC in July 2024 documented APT40's ability to weaponise proof-of-concept exploits against Log4j, Atlassian Confluence and Microsoft Exchange within hours of public disclosure. On 19 July 2021 a US/UK/EU/NATO/Japan/Australia/New Zealand/Canada joint statement formally attributed the ProxyLogon operations to MSS-affiliated actors and singled out the Hainan Xiandun front for its APT40 tasking.

attribution.text: Attributed to the PRC Ministry of State Security's Hainan State Security Department (HSSD), operating through the Hainan Xiandun Technology Development Company front. Attribution has been made by the US Department of Justice through a July 2021 indictment naming three HSSD officers and one Hainan Xiandun contractor, by the US Department of State and a coalition of allies on the same day, by the UK NCSC, by ASD's Australian Cyber Security Centre in AA24-190A, and reinforced by MITRE ATT&CK, Mandiant, Microsoft, Proofpoint, CrowdStrike and Cisco Talos.

name: Evasive Panda
description: Multi-platform: Windows, macOS, Android, Linux, Solaris. Macma backdoor. CloudScout targeting Taiwan.

overview: Evasive Panda is a China-nexus cyber-espionage cluster tracked by MITRE ATT&CK as G1034 under the primary name Daggerfly, and known in vendor reporting as Evasive Panda (ESET), BRONZE HIGHLAND (Secureworks), StormBamboo and StormCloud (Volexity). The group has been active since at least 2012 and is uniquely associated with the MgBot modular framework, which has remained its signature Windows implant across more than a decade of intrusions.

The group's targeting is Chinese-strategic in shape: Tibetan diaspora organisations and the Central Tibetan Administration; Hong Kong pro-democracy activists; individuals, government bodies and NGOs across mainland China, Taiwan, Vietnam, Myanmar and other ASEAN neighbours; and at least one telecommunications carrier in Africa. Reporting from ESET, Symantec's Threat Hunter Team, Volexity and Recorded Future consistently frames the collection interest as internal-security / Ministry of State Security-adjacent — dissidents, religious minorities, and diplomatic and telecom targets whose data supports domestic surveillance rather than economic espionage.

Evasive Panda is one of the few Chinese clusters that operates seriously across every major desktop and mobile platform. MgBot and the Nightdoor / Suzafk backdoor cover Windows; MACMA (also written MacMa) and the GIMMICK framework covered by Volexity in 2022 cover macOS; the Symantec Threat Hunter Team's July 2024 write-up documents Linux and Solaris variants of the group's toolkit alongside an Android tool; and the 2020 Malwarebytes disclosure of a new MgBot variant against India and Hong Kong showed the same operator reusing MgBot's plug-in model across Windows and Android drops. This platform breadth is what lets the group ride ISP-level DNS poisoning and update-channel abuse into whatever the victim happens to be running.

Its signature initial-access technique is supply-chain and update-channel abuse. ESET's April 2023 report documented three years of poisoned automatic updates for popular Chinese software — including Tencent QQ, Sogou Pinyin and other update channels — used to drop MgBot on victims in China's Tibetan community between 2020 and 2022. In August 2024 Volexity attributed to the StormBamboo tag a case in which the operators compromised an unnamed internet service provider and DNS-poisoned software-update lookups to deliver MgBot, MACMA and POCOSTICK/Suzafk to Windows and macOS victims. The same operator, tracked by Volexity as StormCloud, was seen in March 2022 delivering the macOS GIMMICK backdoor to a US-based religious non-profit with Chinese operations. Public reporting has not tied Evasive Panda directly to a named MSS bureau or front company, but Symantec and ESET describe the cluster as long-lived, well-resourced and consistent with a state-sponsored PRC actor.

attribution.text: China-nexus, state-sponsored espionage actor. MITRE ATT&CK's G1034 entry describes Daggerfly / Evasive Panda / BRONZE HIGHLAND as a People's Republic of China-linked APT active since at least 2012 and uniquely associated with the MgBot malware family. ESET, Symantec's Threat Hunter Team and Volexity all characterise the operator as a well-resourced Chinese state-sponsored group targeting internal-security-relevant victims — Tibetans, Hong Kong activists, ASEAN governments and telecoms — but no government has publicly named a specific MSS bureau or front company for the cluster.
attribution.note: No public government indictment or sanctions have named a specific PRC organisation for Evasive Panda / Daggerfly at time of writing; the China-state framing rests on MITRE, ESET, Symantec and Volexity consensus, not on a formal country-level indictment.

name: Tick
description: Japan-focused. Lanscope zero-day CVE-2025-61932 exploitation. Gokcpdoor, OAED Loader. Intellectual property theft.

overview: Tick, tracked by Sophos/Secureworks Counter Threat Unit as BRONZE BUTLER, by Trend Micro as REDBALDKNETIGHT, by CrowdStrike as Stalker Panda, and by Microsoft as Swirl Typhoon, is a long-running China-nexus cyber-espionage cluster whose signature target has been Japan. First observed by Symantec around 2008 and publicly named in 2016, the group has spent close to two decades collecting intellectual property from Japanese heavy industry, defence contractors, aerospace, chemical and biotech firms, IT and managed-services providers, government agencies and media outlets, with secondary interest in South Korea, Taiwan, Russia and Singapore.

Public reporting from Secureworks CTU, Trend Micro, JPCERT/CC, LAC, Cybereason and Palo Alto Unit 42 converges on a bespoke, Japan-adapted toolkit: the Daserf/POSTC backdoor family (also known as Postbot / Muirim), the Datper C2 implant, the xxmm/ShadowWali downloader family, the Minzen framework, and small custom loaders such as ABK, BBK, Nioupale and Ghostdown. Delivery has ranged from targeted spearphishing with weaponised Word/Excel attachments (frequent abuse of the Ichitaro / Sanshiro / Just Systems office-suite exploits favoured in Japan) to watering-hole attacks against Japanese-language sites and, in later years, supply-chain compromise of software widely deployed inside Japanese enterprises.

Tradecraft catalogued across the Secureworks, Trend Micro RedBaldKnight and JPCERT/CC Datper reports includes DLL search-order hijacking against legitimate security-vendor binaries, steganographic staging of second-stage payloads inside PNG/JPG images (documented by Trend Micro in 2017), UAC bypass, Mimikatz / gsecdump / Windows Credential Editor for LSASS dumping, Kerberos ticket forgery, and password-protected RAR archives shipped over HTTP/HTTPS C2 with RC4 and AES obfuscation. Post-2019 activity documented by Trend Micro (Operation ENDTRADE) added a heavier reliance on ShadowPad-family backdoors and multi-stage loaders to hit Japanese defence and heavy-industry supply chains.

Later campaigns broadened the toolkit and target set: Cybereason's ShadowWali write-up and JPCERT/CC's Datper telemetry documented ongoing 2017-2019 activity against Japanese and South Korean organisations, ESET's March 2023 disclosure detailed a supply-chain compromise of a data-loss-prevention software developer in East Asia (with victims across manufacturing, engineering and technology), and 2025 Japanese-vendor and JPCERT/CC coordinated advisories tied Tick to in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2025-61932 in Motex Lanscope Endpoint Manager, paired with a new Go-based Gokcpdoor backdoor and the OAED Loader.

attribution.text: Suspected Chinese state-sponsored cyber-espionage actor. MITRE ATT&CK, Sophos/Secureworks CTU, Trend Micro, JPCERT/CC and Microsoft's threat-actor naming taxonomy all place Tick / BRONZE BUTLER / REDBALDKNETIGHT / Swirl Typhoon in the China cluster; MITRE describes the group as 'suspected Chinese origin' and Microsoft's Swirl Typhoon designation follows its typhoon = China convention. No indictment or government sanctions have publicly named a specific PLA or MSS unit for Tick.
attribution.note: China-nexus attribution is consistent across vendors, but no formal state-level indictment exists; the strongest evidence remains toolkit, target-selection and infrastructure analysis rather than signals intelligence.

origin.text: First observed activity in 2006-2008 per Symantec and MITRE. Secureworks CTU dates its earliest BRONZE BUTLER telemetry to 2008 and links the group to intrusions into Japanese critical infrastructure and heavy-industry manufacturers throughout the 2010s. Trend Micro and Palo Alto Unit 42 corroborate a first-observed date in the 2008-2011 window based on Daserf sample compilation timestamps and campaign infrastructure reuse.

mandate.text: Intellectual-property theft and long-dwell intelligence collection against Japan-headquartered organisations of strategic value to Beijing: defence contractors and aerospace, chemical and biotech firms, semiconductor and electronics manufacturers, IT/managed-services providers, government and media. Secondary targeting reaches South Korea, Taiwan, Russia and Singapore, generally following supply-chain paths back into the Japanese target set. Recent (2023-2025) operations extend the mandate to compromising Japanese-market DLP/endpoint-management software vendors to reach their downstream enterprise customers.

notableOperations.name: REDBALDKNETIGHT steganography campaign
notableOperations.summary: Trend Micro documented a shift in tradecraft in which Tick / REDBALDKNETIGHT concealed the second stage of Daserf inside PNG and JPG images downloaded from attacker-controlled servers, using classic LSB steganography paired with DLL side-loading. The technique defeated many perimeter-DPI signatures that were keyed on plaintext Daserf headers.

notableOperations.name: Datper C2 evolution
notableOperations.summary: JPCERT/CC and Trend Micro tracked the Datper backdoor - a Tick staple written in Delphi/C++ with encoded HTTP GET/POST beacons - across multiple compilation waves aimed at Japanese and South Korean organisations. JPCERT/CC's 2017 proxy-log playbook and 2019 activity report published the URL patterns and MZ-header markers defenders use to detect Datper in the wild.

name: APT31
attribution: PRC Ministry of State Security, Hubei State Security Department (Wuhan XRZ front company)
description: Chinese state-sponsored group tied to the Ministry of State Security's Hubei bureau. Formally attributed by the US DoJ in March 2024 through the indictment of seven operatives working from the Wuhan XRZ front company. Long-running espionage against government officials, journalists, dissidents, and defence and aerospace targets; also the group behind the September 2026 BlueMoon Chrome patch-gap operation Volexity/Proofpoint tracked as JungleBamboo / TA412.

overview: APT31 is a People's Republic of China state-sponsored cyber-espionage group that has operated for at least 15 years, with early activity documented as far back as 2010 by CrowdStrike and Google. The US Department of Justice attributes the group to the Ministry of State Security's Hubei State Security Department (HSSD), operating in practice through a front company named Wuhan Xiaoruizhi Science and Technology Company (Wuhan XRZ).

The group is one of the most heavily aliased actors in threat intelligence: MITRE's canonical listing is ZIRCONIUM/APT31/Violet Typhoon/Judgment Panda/Bronze Vinewood, and public reporting also names it TA412 (Proofpoint) and JungleBamboo (Volexity). In July 2026 Google Threat Intelligence Group added TIDE CASTLE as its own cryptonym under a new naming scheme. This post treats those names as aliases for the same cluster.

APT31's mandate is broad: strategic intelligence collection for the MSS, industrial espionage against defence and aerospace supply chains, and targeting of political figures, journalists and human-rights organisations perceived as critics of the PRC. Where APT41 mixes espionage with financially motivated intrusions, APT31 is consistently espionage-only.

attribution.text: Attributed to the PRC Ministry of State Security's Hubei State Security Department, operating through the Wuhan XRZ front company. name: Scattered Spider
description: Young English-speaking threat actors specializing in social engineering, SIM swapping, and MFA fatigue attacks. Responsible for MGM Resorts and Caesars Entertainment breaches. Partnered with BlackCat/ALPHV for ransomware deployment.

overview: Scattered Spider is a loosely-affiliated, English-speaking financially motivated cybercrime collective active since at least May 2022. It is not a company or a formal syndicate: reporting from Mandiant/Google, Microsoft, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Unit 42 and CISA all treat the name as an umbrella over a shifting set of overlapping personas rooted in the broader 'The Com' (or 'Comm') ecosystem â the same Anglophone SIM-swap and social-engineering underground that also spawned Lapsus$. Every major vendor has its own cryptonym for the cluster: UNC3944 (Mandiant), Octo Tempest and Storm-0875 (Microsoft), Muddled Libra (Palo Alto Unit 42), Roasted 0ktapus (Group-IB), Star Fraud, Scatter Swine and Oktapus.

The group's defining trait is an identity-first tradecraft that walks past EDR because there is essentially nothing to detect on the endpoint. Initial access is typically obtained through voice social engineering against IT help desks â impersonating a legitimate employee, feeding correct PII scraped from data brokers or previous breaches, and requesting a password or MFA reset â supplemented by SMS phishing (smishing), MFA-fatigue push bombing, and, historically, SIM swapping. Once inside, operators favour legitimate remote-management tooling (AnyDesk, TeamViewer, Splashtop, ScreenConnect, ngrok, Chisel, Teleport) and living-off-the-land binaries, and pivot fast into SaaS and cloud control planes (Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Azure, AWS, Snowflake, vCenter, CyberArk, Salesforce).

Its monetisation model has evolved through three affiliations with Russian-speaking ransomware programs â a notable inversion of the historical rule that Eastern European ransomware crews refused to work with native English speakers. From mid-2023 the group deployed BlackCat/ALPHV on VMware ESXi in the MGM Resorts and Caesars Entertainment intrusions; after ALPHV's February 2024 exit scam it moved to RansomHub as an affiliate from June 2024 (ReliaQuest); and by April 2025 it was operating with DragonForce, the encryptor used in the M&S, Co-op and Harrods intrusions.

Public arrests through 2024-2026 have not slowed the cluster: Noah Michael Urban ('King Bob/Sosa') pleaded guilty in 2024 and was sentenced to 10 years in August 2025; five defendants including Tyler Robert Buchanan were charged in November 2024 in the Central District of California; Buchanan was extradited from Spain in April 2025 and pleaded guilty in April 2026; UK national Thalha Jubair was charged in the District of New Jersey in September 2025 in connection with 120 intrusions and over $115M in ransom payments; and Peter Stokes was arrested in Finland and extradited in April 2026. Through 2025-2026 the collective has run consecutive sector campaigns â UK retail (April-May 2025), US insurance (May-June 2025) and aviation (June-July 2025) â and the joint CISA/FBI advisory AA23-320A was updated on 29 July 2025 to reflect the DragonForce shift.

attribution.text: Not state-sponsored. A loosely-organised, financially motivated collective of predominantly English-speaking (US/UK/Canada) actors overlapping with 'The Com'. Mandiant tracks it as UNC3944, Microsoft as Octo Tempest/Storm-0875, CrowdStrike as Scattered Spider, Palo Alto Unit 42 as Muddled Libra. Multiple US and UK indictments and arrests have named individual operators.

techniques.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Voice

techniques.name: Phishing (Mobile)
techniques.usage: SMS smishing waves ('your account will be deactivated, click here') directing employees to typosquat SSO portals with adversary-in-the-middle credential/OTP capture. The 0ktapus campaign phished 130+ organisations this way in 2022.

techniques.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
techniques.usage: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing. Repeatedly triggers Duo/Authenticator push notifications until the victim approves one, often paired with a vishing call framing the pushes as a legitimate 'sync issue'.

techniques.name: SIM Card Swap
techniques.usage: Historical bread-and-butter (Star Fraud era). Bribes or social-engineers telco employees to port the victim's number to an attacker-controlled SIM, intercepting SMS OTPs. Basis of the Urban / Buchanan indictments.

techniques.name: Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts
techniques.usage: Post-reset access to Microsoft Entra ID, Okta and AWS/Azure accounts is the group's primary form of persistence â no malware needed. Frequently self-assigns Global Administrator / Okta super-admin.

techniques.name: Modify Authentication Process: Multi-Factor Authentication
techniques.usage: After account takeover, registers attacker-controlled MFA tokens on the victim account so subsequent access no longer requires social engineering â the standard identity-first persistence primitive.

techniques.name: Modify Authentication Process: Conditional Access Policies
techniques.usage: Adds attacker IP ranges / geolocations to Azure AD conditional access 'trusted locations' to exempt itself from step-up MFA policies while remaining below the radar of anomaly rules.

techniques.name: Account Manipulation: Device Registration
techniques.usage: Registers attacker-controlled devices to compromised accounts, using them to satisfy device-compliance conditional-access rules and to sign in through the victim VPN as a trusted endpoint.

techniques.name: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification: Trust Modification
techniques.usage: Adds rogue federated identity providers to Microsoft Entra ID (Golden SAML). Enables the operator to mint arbitrary user tokens against the tenant without knowing any password.

techniques.name: Remote Access Tools
techniques.usage: Prefers legitimate RMM tooling over custom malware: AnyDesk, TeamViewer, Splashtop, LogMeIn, ScreenConnect/ConnectWise, ngrok, Chisel, RustDesk, Teleport. Delivered by walking the user through installation over the vishing call.

name: LockBit
description: Formerly the most prolific RaaS operation. Disrupted by Operation Cronos (FBI/Europol) in February 2024. Leader Dmitry Khoroshev identified and sanctioned. Over 2,000 victims with $120M+ in ransom payments collected.

overview: LockBit is a Russia-nexus ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation active from September 2019 until it was disrupted by Operation Cronos on 19 February 2024. It began life as "ABCD" ransomware, renamed to LockBit later that year, and iterated through three named encryptor generations: LockBit 1.0 (2019-2021), LockBit 2.0 / LockBit Red (mid-2021, adding the StealBit exfiltration utility and the group's first double-extortion leak site), and LockBit 3.0 / LockBit Black (June 2022, notable for launching the first public bug bounty program run by a ransomware crew). A fourth strain, LockBit Green (January 2023), was a rebadged Conti v3 encryptor offered to affiliates coming off the collapsed Conti program.

For roughly three years LockBit was the single most prolific ransomware brand on the planet. CISA's June 2023 joint advisory AA23-165A attributed 1,700 US intrusions and roughly $91 million in US ransom payments to LockBit affiliates since 2020; the UK National Crime Agency's Operation Cronos take-down said the operation had extracted more than $1 billion globally from over 7,000 victims. Notable victims include Accenture (2021), the UK's Royal Mail (January 2023), a TSMC supplier (June 2023), Boeing (October 2023), the US arm of the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (November 2023) and Fulton County, Georgia (January 2024).

On 19-20 February 2024, a joint operation led by the UK NCA with the US FBI, Europol and law-enforcement partners from ten additional countries seized 34 LockBit servers across three continents, took control of the group's Tor leak site and rebranded it into a countdown-to-disclosure page, released a decryptor through the No More Ransom portal and arrested two affiliates in Poland and Ukraine. On 7 May 2024 a follow-up unsealed a US District of New Jersey indictment naming the "LockBitSupp" administrator as Dmitry Yuryevich Khoroshev, a 31-year-old Russian national; the US Treasury, UK Foreign Office and Australian government sanctioned him the same day.

LockBit briefly attempted to relaunch after the take-down, standing up new .onion sites and posting fabricated "new" victim lists composed largely of old data. The operation never recovered its affiliate base, which migrated to RansomHub, Play, Akira, BlackSuit and DragonForce. As of the 2026 verification date the LockBit brand is effectively dormant, though Khoroshev remains at large in Russia and the RaaS panel source code, leaked in 2022 by a disgruntled developer, continues to seed forks used by lower-tier crews.

attribution.text: Russia-based ransomware-as-a-service operation run by "LockBitSupp", identified by the US Department of Justice, UK NCA, UK Foreign Office and Australian government on 7 May 2024 as Dmitry Yuryevich Khoroshev (born 17 April 1993, Voronezh, Russia). No formal state-sponsorship link has been established, but the group's affiliate rules explicitly forbid targeting former USSR entities — a pattern consistent with tacit Russian-state tolerance of domestic ransomware crews.

origin.text: First observed as "ABCD" ransomware in September 2019, renamed LockBit before the end of that year. LockBit 2.0 launched in mid-2021 as the affiliate program matured; LockBit 3.0 / Black shipped in June 2022 and introduced the ransomware world's first bug bounty program. LockBit Green appeared in January 2023 as a rebadged Conti v3 build targeted at ex-Conti affiliates.

sources.title: AA23-165A: Understanding Ransomware Threat Actors: LockBit

mandate.text: Purely financially motivated. Operates as an affiliate-driven RaaS: the core team supplies the encryptor, the leak site, StealBit for exfiltration and negotiation infrastructure; affiliates run the intrusions and keep the majority of the ransom. Affiliate rules exclude CIS-country targets, forbid attacks on critical services in most jurisdictions in name only, and are enforced through public reputation-management on Khoroshev's forum persona LockBitSupp.

notableOperations.name: Royal Mail international export services disruption
notableOperations.summary: On 11 January 2023 a LockBit affiliate encrypted Royal Mail's international export systems, halting all overseas letter and parcel shipments from the UK for six weeks. LockBit's negotiator initially demanded roughly $80 million; the exchange between Royal Mail's team and "LockBitSupp" leaked in February 2023 and Royal Mail publicly refused to pay. It was the highest-profile UK critical-services ransomware incident of the year.

Boeing refused to pay and LockBit leaked roughly 43 GB of Boeing data on 10 November; ICBC's US Treasury settlement operations were forced offline, forcing manual settlement of billions of dollars in trades.

LockBit's data-leak countdown expired without publication after Operation Cronos took down the leak site three weeks later.

techniques.usage: Affiliates routinely buy access from initial-access brokers on Russian-language forums — stolen VPN, RDP and Citrix credentials are the single most common LockBit entry vector.

techniques.usage: Weaponised CVE-2023-4966 (CitrixBleed) against NetScaler ADC in the Boeing/ICBC campaign; also observed exploiting Fortinet FortiOS (CVE-2018-13379), F5 BIG-IP (CVE-2022-1388) and ManageEngine ADSelfService Plus.

techniques.name: External Remote Services
techniques.usage: Abuses internet-exposed RDP, VPN and remote-management gateways — the affiliate CISA-documented case backlog lists dozens of incidents rooted in an exposed RDP host.

techniques.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
techniques.usage: Affiliates deliver LockBit through malicious Office documents and ISO/LNK attachments in targeted email campaigns, often chained after a Qakbot or IcedID loader.

techniques.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
techniques.usage: Uses PowerShell for reconnaissance, tooling download and encryptor deployment; the CISA advisory lists dozens of specific commands captured across engagements.

techniques.name: Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
techniques.usage: LockBit 3.0 registers scheduled tasks on all reachable hosts to trigger the encryptor at a synchronised time across the estate.

techniques.name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Bypass User Account Control
techniques.usage: LockBit 3.0 bypasses UAC through the CMSTPLUA COM elevation and, in variants, ICMLuaUtil, to obtain high-integrity execution before encryption.

techniques.name: Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading
techniques.usage: SentinelLabs documented a LockBit affiliate side-loading Cobalt Strike Beacon through the legitimately signed VMware xfer.exe utility.

sources.title: LockBit side-loads Cobalt Strike with VMware xfer.exe

techniques.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
techniques.usage: Runs Defender-Control, PCHunter and custom scripts to disable EDR agents and Windows Defender before dropping the encryptor. Kills 200+ named services and processes.

techniques.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
techniques.usage: LockBit 3.0 requires a 32-byte password passed at command line to decrypt its own strings and unpack the payload — an anti-analysis measure that stalled sandbox coverage for months.

techniques.name: OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory
techniques.usage: Mimikatz and comsvcs.dll MiniDump are the go-to LSASS-dumping tools across LockBit affiliate playbooks documented by CISA and vendors.

techniques.name: Remote System Discovery
techniques.usage: Uses Advanced IP Scanner, SoftPerfect Network Scanner and PowerShell AD enumeration (ADFind, ADRecon) to map the domain before lateral movement.

techniques.name: Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
techniques.usage: RDP is the affiliate lateral-movement default; observed alongside AnyDesk, Splashtop and Atera in Talos IR engagements.

techniques.name: Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
techniques.usage: PsExec and SMB admin shares deliver the encryptor to hundreds of hosts in the endgame; LockBit 2.0 propagated automatically via Active Directory group policy.

techniques.name: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
techniques.usage: StealBit — the group's bespoke exfiltration tool — uploads to attacker-controlled S3 buckets and MEGA. Affiliates are also known to abuse Rclone and FileZilla for the same purpose.

techniques.name: Data Encrypted for Impact
techniques.usage: AES-256-CBC file encryption with an RSA-2048 wrapped key; extension .lockbit or a randomised HKID (LockBit 3.0). Cross-platform builds cover Windows, Linux and VMware ESXi.

techniques.name: Service Stop
techniques.usage: Terminates SQL Server, Exchange, backup-agent and hypervisor services before encryption to unlock files for the encryptor thread.

techniques.name: Inhibit System Recovery
techniques.usage: Deletes shadow copies via vssadmin, disables Windows Recovery Environment and clears the event log. LockBit Green additionally purges Veeam and Acronis backup configurations.

techniques.name: Financial Theft
techniques.usage: Double-extortion revenue model: leak-site publication or auction of stolen data if the ransom is not paid. Chainalysis attributed roughly $500M in ransom collections to LockBit through 2023.

name: BlackCat/ALPHV
description: First Rust-based ransomware. Cross-platform (Windows, Linux, VMware ESXi). Exit scammed after $22M Change Healthcare ransom. FBI seized infrastructure December 2023 but group briefly resumed operations.

overview: BlackCat, also tracked as ALPHV and Noberus, was a Russia-nexus ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation first observed on Russian-language cybercrime forums in November 2021. The programme is best known as the first widely-deployed ransomware written in Rust: a cross-platform, Windows/Linux/VMware ESXi build with a per-victim configuration blob, JSON-based tasking and a heavily-marketed affiliate console. Mandiant tracks its most prolific affiliate cluster as UNC4466; Microsoft threat intel reports both the RaaS core and multiple affiliate clusters under DEV-* and Storm-* aliases; and Palo Alto Unit 42, Group-IB, Trend Micro, Symantec, CrowdStrike and Kaspersky all published parallel technical write-ups within the group's first six months.

The core team is the direct successor to the DarkSide RaaS (May 2020) and its BlackMatter rebrand (July-November 2021). DarkSide was the operation behind the May 2021 Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack that triggered a US East Coast fuel emergency; after DarkSide shut down under US law-enforcement pressure the same operators surfaced as BlackMatter, then, once BlackMatter was themselves disrupted in November 2021, launched BlackCat/ALPHV with a rewritten Rust locker and a revised affiliate split. CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Unit 42 and Group-IB all documented code, infrastructure and tradecraft overlaps linking the three programmes to the CARBON SPIDER / FIN7-adjacent cluster of Russian-speaking operators.

BlackCat's business model was affiliate-driven big-game hunting: initial access brokered by third parties (often Scattered Spider / Octo Tempest social-engineering crews, or exploitation clusters like UNC4466 abusing Veritas Backup Exec), then hands-on-keyboard escalation, data exfiltration with the custom ExMatter/Fendr tool, and double-extortion detonation of the Rust locker across Windows, Linux and ESXi hosts. Marquee incidents included the September 2023 attacks on MGM Resorts International and Caesars Entertainment (with Scattered Spider affiliates), the April 2023 Western Digital compromise, a Reddit data theft disclosed in June 2023, and the February 2024 attack on Change Healthcare, a UnitedHealth Group subsidiary that processes roughly one third of US medical claims.

On 19 December 2023 the US Department of Justice, FBI, CISA and international partners announced Operation-level disruption of the BlackCat/ALPHV infrastructure: the FBI seized the group's Tor negotiation and leak sites, developed a decryption tool that was offered to more than 500 victims, and joint FBI/CISA/HHS advisory AA23-353A published the full IOC/TTP set. The operators briefly 'unseized' a mirror site and continued to accept affiliate work, but the programme collapsed on 5 March 2024 when, after receiving a reported $22M ransom from a Change Healthcare affiliate ('notchy'), the BlackCat core team walked off with the payment, faked an FBI reseizure banner and shut down operations in what is now the canonical example of a RaaS exit scam. Most former affiliates migrated to RansomHub during 2024.

attribution.text: Russia-nexus, financially motivated criminal enterprise; no state sponsor identified. Core operators are the same cluster that ran the DarkSide (2020-2021) and BlackMatter (2021) RaaS programmes — publicly tracked by CrowdStrike as CARBON SPIDER, by Mandiant as UNC4466 for its most prolific affiliate, and by Group-IB, Palo Alto Unit 42, Symantec and Microsoft under matching descriptions of a Russian-speaking, FIN7-adjacent operator group. Members are believed to operate from Russia and the CIS on the basis of programme rules that forbid targeting of CIS-country victims, Russian-language recruitment ads, and forum artefacts documented by Group-IB.

name: RansomHub
attribution: Russia-nexus RaaS (Cyclops → Knight rebrand; CIS-exempt affiliate rules)
description: Rapidly growing RaaS operation that absorbed former LockBit and BlackCat affiliates after those operations collapsed. Golang-based ransomware with cross-platform support. Notable victims include Change Healthcare data re-extortion.

overview: RansomHub is a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) operation that launched its affiliate programme in February 2024 and, within nine months, became the single most prolific ransomware brand tracked on public leak sites. The CISA/FBI/HHS/MS-ISAC joint advisory AA24-242A of 29 August 2024 formally states that RansomHub is a rebrand of the earlier Knight ransomware, which was itself a re-tooling of the 2023 Cyclops family. Symantec's Threat Hunter Team, Group-IB and SentinelLabs independently confirm this Cyclops -> Knight -> RansomHub lineage through code and infrastructure overlap.

The group's rise was structural, not accidental. In late February 2024 the ALPHV/BlackCat operation carried out an exit scam after receiving the roughly USD 22 million Change Healthcare ransom, refusing to pay the affiliate ("Notchy") who had done the intrusion. Weeks later Operation Cronos disrupted LockBit. RansomHub launched an affiliate programme with an unusual 90 percent affiliate cut and a prepayment model that routed victim payments directly to affiliates first, and absorbed the bulk of the newly unattached BlackCat and LockBit affiliates, including Notchy, who publicly re-extorted UnitedHealth by listing Change Healthcare data on RansomHub's leak site in April 2024.

Operationally the group runs a Rust-based cross-platform encryptor (Windows, Linux, ESXi, FreeBSD, ARM) that uses Curve25519 for key exchange and ChaCha20 or AES for file encryption, with an intermittent-encryption option. Affiliates rely heavily on stolen valid accounts and edge-device exploitation (Citrix NetScaler, FortiOS, Zerologon-era Windows), then chain LSA/ntds.dit dumping, PsExec-style lateral movement, AnyDesk / Atera / Splashtop / ConnectWise for remote access, and Rclone / WinSCP / MEGA for exfiltration. Signature EDR-evasion tools include a custom EDRKillShifter driver-loader documented by Sophos and Trend Micro, and abuse of Kaspersky's legitimately signed TDSSKiller utility.

Attribution to a specific state or criminal umbrella is not publicly established. The affiliate programme forbids attacks against CIS/Russia, Cuba, North Korea and China, which is the traditional Russophone-ecosystem tell, and multiple affiliates known to be Russian-speaking former BlackCat/LockBit operators have joined. Microsoft has also documented North Korean Onyx Sleet / Moonstone Sleet activity deploying RansomHub payloads. In practice RansomHub is best treated as a Russia-nexus criminal service platform with a broad, cross-nationality affiliate roster rather than a single crew.

attribution.text: Russophone-ecosystem RaaS operation of unknown ownership, launched as a rebrand of Knight (formerly Cyclops) ransomware in February 2024 and running an affiliate model that explicitly forbids attacks against CIS states. CISA, FBI, HHS and MS-ISAC jointly attribute the RaaS brand; Symantec, Group-IB and SentinelLabs corroborate the Knight/Cyclops lineage through code overlap. Microsoft has separately documented DPRK-nexus Moonstone Sleet deploying RansomHub payloads as an affiliate.

name: Black Basta
description: Formed by former Conti ransomware members. Known for Microsoft Teams-based social engineering and Quick Assist abuse for initial access. Over 500 organizations targeted across 12+ countries.

overview: Black Basta is a Russia-nexus, Russian-speaking ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation that surfaced in April 2022 and quickly became one of the most prolific big-game-hunting crews of the 2022-2025 period. Unlike open-affiliate programs such as LockBit or REvil, Black Basta has consistently run a small, insider affiliate model: recruitment is by invitation from a core group of Russian-speaking operators, and public reporting from Trend Micro, Sophos, SentinelOne, Palo Alto Unit 42 and Mandiant (Google Cloud) all point to substantial overlap in tradecraft, infrastructure and personnel with the former Conti ransomware group, which shut down its main brand in May 2022 in the wake of the Ukraine-war chat leaks.

Mandiant tracks the primary Black Basta operators as UNC4393; Microsoft tracks a closely-aligned Teams-vishing affiliate as Storm-1811 (later Storm-2410). Initial access up to August 2023 rode almost entirely on the Qakbot / Qbot loader botnet, and Black Basta's operational rhythm was disrupted when the FBI's Operation Duck Hunt seized Qakbot infrastructure. From late 2023 the group pivoted to Pikabot, DarkGate, IcedID and ScreenConnect abuse, and from November 2023 UNC4393-linked affiliates began mass-emailing corporate users with newsletter-bomb floods followed by fake IT-help-desk Microsoft Teams chats and Quick Assist screen-sharing sessions — the campaign that CISA, FBI, HHS and MS-ISAC covered in joint advisory AA24-131A in May 2024.

The group's victimology is broad but tilts heavily toward North American and European manufacturing, healthcare, construction and professional services. Publicly-known incidents include the American Dental Association (April 2022, one of the group's first major listings), Rheinmetall (April 2023), ABB (May 2023), Yellow Corporation (Sept 2023, weeks before the trucker filed for bankruptcy), Sobeys, Capita, Hyundai Motor Europe and Ascension Health — a 140-hospital Catholic system in the US whose May 2024 outage forced ambulance diversions and manual clinical workflows across multiple states. CISA's May 2024 advisory documented more than 500 victims across 12+ countries and every one of the 16 US critical-infrastructure sectors.

In February 2025 an actor using the alias 'ExploitWhispers' dumped roughly a year of Black Basta's internal Matrix chats onto Telegram and MEGA, an event widely compared to the 2022 Conti leak. PRODAFT, Kaspersky (Securelist), Trellix and Arctic Wolf analyses of the corpus documented the group's affiliate onboarding, negotiation playbooks, ties to Cactus Team and the Qakbot / DarkGate loader crews, and reported internal friction after the Ascension attack drew federal scrutiny. Public leak-site postings dropped sharply through 2025 and by mid-year several trackers had reclassified the operation as effectively dormant under the Black Basta brand, with likely successor activity spinning up under new names.

attribution.text: Russian-speaking, financially motivated RaaS operation widely assessed as a Conti-successor cluster. Mandiant tracks the operator group as UNC4393; Microsoft tracks the Teams-vishing affiliate as Storm-1811 (rebranded Storm-2410 in mid-2024). Attribution has been reinforced by the joint CISA/FBI/HHS/MS-ISAC advisory AA24-131A, by Mandiant's UNC4393 profile, and by the February 2025 internal chat leak analysed by PRODAFT, Kaspersky and Trellix.

origin.text: First observed in April 2022 with the launch of the Basta News data-leak site. The American Dental Association incident, disclosed on 22 April 2022, is one of the earliest publicly confirmed intrusions. Multiple vendors (SentinelOne, Trend Micro, Palo Alto Unit 42) place the operational start within weeks of the May 2022 Conti brand shutdown, and the February 2025 chat leak shows internal continuity with Conti personnel.

mandate.text: Financial gain via double-extortion ransomware: bulk data theft followed by symmetric encryption of Windows and VMware ESXi hosts, with a Basta News leak site used to pressure non-paying victims. No political or espionage mandate observed. Ransom demands routinely into the seven- and eight-figure range; Chainalysis estimated the operation cleared more than USD 100M in on-chain payments during 2022-2023 alone.

notableOperations.name: Qakbot pivot after Operation Duck Hunt
notableOperations.summary: Black Basta's primary loader for its first sixteen months of activity was Qakbot / Qbot. On 29 August 2023 the FBI and international partners announced Operation Duck Hunt, a multi-country takedown that seized Qakbot's infrastructure and pushed an uninstaller to more than 700,000 infected hosts. UNC4393 rotated to DarkGate, IcedID, Pikabot and SilentNight, and Mandiant reports the affiliate slowed noticeably during the transition — by mid-2024 the operators had converged on a bespoke SystemBC-plus-Cobalt-Strike loader stack.

notableOperations.name: Microsoft Teams vishing and Quick Assist abuse (Storm-1811)
notableOperations.summary: From late 2023 through 2024, Black Basta affiliates flooded targeted users with newsletter-subscription bombing, then contacted them over Microsoft Teams from attacker-controlled tenants impersonating internal IT help desks. Operators walked victims into launching Windows Quick Assist (built-in remote support), took control of the endpoint, dropped SystemBC, ScreenConnect and Cobalt Strike, and moved to ransomware within hours. CISA/FBI issued AA24-131A on 10 May 2024 and Microsoft published a dedicated Storm-1811 write-up five days later; Rapid7 tracked ongoing waves through August 2024.

notableOperations.name: Ascension Health intrusion
notableOperations.summary: On 8 May 2024 Ascension — a 140-hospital Catholic non-profit spanning 19 US states — disclosed an ongoing cyberattack; internal EHR (Epic), phone systems, patient portals and pharmacy systems were taken offline. Ambulances were diverted for weeks and clinical staff reverted to paper workflows. Public reporting and CISA's AA24-131A advisory linked the attack to Black Basta; Ascension later disclosed that data of nearly 5.6M patients was accessed. Widely regarded as one of the most disruptive US healthcare ransomware events of 2024.
